F083

Weather by the hour: the hourly forecast for home

Needs a buildLow riskAdults and kidsValue 3/5Effort SWave D

Ask whether it will rain at home on Saturday morning and get the chance of rain hour by hour, with any active weather alert for home, straight from the National Weather Service. The evening text and the day-out planner use the same hourly line.

Example: Jordan texts: 'Will it rain at home on Saturday between 9 and noon?' Happy answers with the hourly chance of rain for those hours and any active alert for home.

Backed by National Weather Service: API Web Service documentation weather.gov: The National Weather Service offers hourly forecasts for the next seven days and active alerts as open data, free to use for any purpose, through a service meant for others to build on; opened in this run.

How it works and its limits

How Extend the in-house home_weather plugin: follow forecastHourly from the points lookup the tool already makes, so the tool can also answer hour by hour, on the same pinned host (api.weather.gov), with the same refusal of redirects and of any forecast address on another host. Active alerts are already fetched with every forecast and stay as they are. Not built: a snowfall figure from the raw gridpoint endpoint, and an alert id in the output. The plugin's own tests are extended with a recorded hourly response, and one live question about rain on a given afternoon is answered by the hour before it goes live. No house-rules rule.

Depends on home_weather plugin (exists; this extends it)

Limits

  • Apple's Weather app can already send a notification when rain or snow is about to start or stop, and for government-issued severe-weather alerts at a saved location; Apple notes this is not offered in every country or region. This tool earns its place as the hourly rain line for the evening text (F014) and the day-out planner (F028), and for questions asked inside a Happy conversation.
  • The National Weather Service hourly forecast reaches seven days ahead, so a question about a day further out gets no hour-by-hour answer until the date comes into range.
  • The tool knows only the home point, so it cannot answer for a field or a venue somewhere else; for other places Happy falls back to web search.
  • No snowfall amount in numbers on day one. The field exists in the raw gridpoint data, in millimetres over mostly six-hour intervals, so it would not give an hour-by-hour amount; the forecaster's own text for each period still comes through. It is added only if a first snow forecast shows the need.

Safety Read-only public data from one pinned government host. A lookup sends the home's coordinates and the header that identifies the app, as the National Weather Service asks, and nothing else about the family. What comes back is outside content from a single government source; the tool only reads, and cannot write anything or message anyone.

Not verified

  • What a live hourly response for the home point looks like: the sources cite the weather service's documentation, not a response read for home. The go-live check (one live question about rain on a given afternoon, answered by the hour) settles it.
  • NWS publishes no numeric rate limit, so the 10-minute cache is a design choice rather than an NWS rule.
  • Whether Apple's Weather notifications are offered and switched on for the home location on each parent's iPhone: the Apple page read was the Mac Weather guide, and the iPhone guide did not render.

It would be built together with the weather watch (F018).

Family workflows, digests and monitors built from tier 1. Your example was watching school email and notifying you. 14 are planned.

School and kids 2

F051

School lines first in the weekday 07:00 mail text

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 5/5Effort SWave A

Each parent whose Gmail is connected gets a weekday 07:00 mail text (G015) that opens with the school lines: a short list of the last day's school and activity mail about the two children, with dates spelled out and things to do first. The model picks out the school mail from the whole inbox, with the school's sender addresses as a hint and not as a filter, and passes on no links. Length and layout are tuned on the first two weeks of real mail.

Example: Trigger: the weekday 07:00 mail text, one to each parent from that parent's own inbox. After the job's own label it opens with the school lines, for example: 'Mail. School: picture day is Thursday 15 October, order form due Wednesday 14 October; the third-grader's trip slip is due Friday 16 October.' The other mail lines follow in the same text.

Combines F056 School and activities mail digest (weekdays 16:00): five-line summary, dated checklist, lunch-balance and school-platform lines

Backed by Fambot: AI Family Assistant (App Store listing by Fambot Inc) apps.apple.com: A shipping family assistant sells the same function: it reads school emails and newsletters and sends parents a daily digest of what to know, do and decide; opened in this run.

How it works and its limits

How No separate job, no sender list, no check on the search and no stored last-run marker. The school lines are one instruction in the message of the weekday 07:00 job on each parent's mail reader (G015). The short jobs script (G003) creates that job with the owner's handle read from the family file, a time limit and a tool list of Gmail read tools only. The instruction: from the last day's mail (three days on a Monday), list first what comes from the school district, teachers, teams and activities, each date spelled out, the sender named, no links. One hint line carries the school's sender addresses, which Tony provides at execution. Mail from other senders that is plainly school mail is still listed. After go-live, read the first two weeks of digests to see which school systems actually write; only then change a platform's own digest setting, and only for one that shows up.

Depends on G015 read-only Gmail connection and mail reader, one per parent: the school lines are part of its weekday 07:00 job and go live with it; G003 in its simplified form: the three scheduler switches and the short jobs script; Tony provides the school district's sender addresses at execution (he said he would); they go into the job's message as a hint; Jordan approves read-only Gmail herself on Google's screen (she has agreed), for the school lines in her own text

Limits

  • The model, not a list, decides what counts as school mail, so a school mail can be missed or a non-school mail included. No links are passed on; the parent opens the mail in Gmail.
  • A school mail that arrives during the day is reported the next morning; there is no afternoon text. Whether the school already texts or pushes urgent notices to the parents' phones is not on record.
  • Both parents receive the same school mail, so the school lines in the two texts will mostly match. Each is built from its owner's inbox, and nothing is sent from one parent's reader to the other parent.
  • If a school system emails grades or attendance, that is a child's education record, and it reaches the cloud model with the rest of the mail. Attachments are not opened, so a newsletter sent as a PDF or a picture shows up as a subject line only.
  • A day-before reminder is not wired from the text: the mail reader holds no reminder tool on purpose, because it reads outside mail. Tony types the reminder to his own agent once timed reminders exist (F007); that works for Tony only, because Jordan is not a command owner.
  • Which school systems send this family mail is not on record, so nothing is changed on any school platform until real digests show which ones write.

Safety School mail is outside content. Only its owner's mail reader reads it: Gmail read tools only, no web, file, send or message tool. Once the lookup (G015) is on, the owner's own agent is allowed the same three tools so that the reader it starts can use them, and is told never to use them itself. Its scheduled text goes to its owner alone, and the lookup (G015) returns an answer to that owner's own agent only when the parent asks. No links are relayed. The card needs no rule in the house-rules plugin. Mail text goes to the cloud model, as Tony allowed on 12 Oct.

  • Library overdue and hold-ready notice emails are one more sender class; the full checked-out list stays in the library's own app.

Since the personal-inbox watch was dropped last round, the only list left is the shared school mailbox's, which has no single owner to approve; that becomes one line in the school mailbox item (F051), and no other item depends on this one.

CRT-11

Childcare coverage planner: no-school days and summer weeks

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 4/5Effort MWave ENew

A grid of the weekdays the two children have no school (teacher days, breaks, early releases, summer weeks) against who covers each one. Either parent adds or changes cover by text and can ask what is still open, and a monthly text lists the open days and weeks to each parent who has it switched on, staying silent when nothing is open. The parents register and pay for anything themselves.

Example: Trigger: the monthly text. Each parent who has it switched on gets, for example: 'Coverage still open: Friday 6 November, both children; the week of 5 July for the kindergartner.' Jordan then texts her own Happy: 'the week of 5 July is covered, mark it booked', and the next answer either parent gets shows it.

Backed by Spreadsheets, Waitlists, and Camp Fees: Welcome to the Jordan Care Scramble (Buffett Early Childhood Institute, University of Nebraska) buffettinstitute.nebraska.edu: A university early-childhood institute describes parents building camp spreadsheets months ahead, racing registration openings, landing on waitlists and still having weeks of summer with no cover; opened in this run.

How it works and its limits

How This card adds one coverage table and three tools (add, change, list) to the household database plugin (F031) and keeps no store of its own. A row holds a date range, which child, a status (open, pencilled, booked, paid) and a short who-covers label; the tools accept only those typed fields. No-school days come from the school district's calendar: through the calendar tool (F009) once the family Google calendar is subscribed to its feed, or from a photo or PDF (F002). The parent's agent lists the days and writes rows only after a yes. One monthly job per parent who has it switched on, from the jobs script (G003) and holding only the list tool, texts the open rows to its owner under its own label, or answers NO_REPLY. Registration dates are ordinary reminders (F007, Tony only); camp options are an ordinary question to the research helper (F019). Not built: weekly pre-break jobs, page watches, the receipts list, a house-rules rule.

Depends on F031 household database in its smallest form: this card adds its one coverage table and its three tools there; the rows are shared data both parents' agents write, so they live there and nowhere else; F009 read-only calendar, with the family Google calendar subscribed to the school district's calendar feed; or F002 photo and PDF reading, for a district calendar that exists only as a PDF. Tony provides the feed link or the PDF at execution; G003 in its simplified form: the jobs script creates the monthly text, one job per parent who has it switched on; Tony provides at execution: the day and hour of the monthly text, and which of the two parents have it switched on (one job each); Tony provides a short label for each of the two children at execution (not a full name; the same labels the dose log, CRT-10, uses); Optional, not needed for the grid: F007 reminders for registration dates (Tony only, since Jordan is not a command owner) and F019 research helper for camp options

Limits

  • The planner earns its keep only if both parents have to arrange cover on those days. A shared spreadsheet does the grid; the gain here is asking in the thread and the monthly list of what is open.
  • Registration is a booking and a payment: Happy stops at the reminder and the link, and the parents register and pay.
  • Reminders for registration dates work for Tony only, because Jordan is not a command owner; when she asks, Happy lists the dates and she sets them on her phone.
  • Camp sites are often script-heavy or bot-walled, so an answer about camp options may say 'could not verify'; the parent pastes the dates. Such a question carries ages, weeks and a distance to the research helper, never names or the school.
  • The rows are shared between the two adults by design. Values stay short and typed (a date range, a status, a label), not text lifted from a page or a flyer.
  • No weekly texts before a break and no watch on a camp's registration page; either is added only after the monthly text has proved useful and a parent asks.

Safety Rows are written only through the database plugin's tools, which accept in code only typed fields: dates, a child's label, one of four statuses and a short label. The district calendar or flyer is outside content, so rows are written only after a yes. The monthly job holds one read tool and texts only its owner. Nothing is registered, booked or paid.

Not verified

  • Whether the school district publishes a calendar feed or only a PDF.
  • That events from a calendar subscribed by link are returned through the Google Calendar API, and so through gog's calendar tool.
  • That a tool from the in-house household-database plugin can be named in a job's tool list; the installed docs show the <server>__<tool> form for MCP servers only.
  • That the monthly job on an empty grid sends nothing and raises no failure alert: a hand-started run before go-live shows it.

Daily briefs and digests 1

F014

Evening text at 21:00 Eastern: tomorrow's calendar and the weather

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 5/5Effort SWave C

At 21:00 Eastern Tony gets one text built from the family's shared Google calendar and the weather: tomorrow's events, the forecast for home and any active weather alert, and no text at all when nothing is on. Its Sunday run covers the week ahead. Jordan's copy is one more job on her own agent when she has it switched on.

Example: On an evening before a day with two calendar events, Tony gets one text at 21:00: the two events with their times, and 'rain likely in the afternoon'. On an evening before an empty day he gets nothing.

Backed by Schedule actions in Gemini Apps - Gemini Apps Help support.google.com: Google's own assistant offers scheduled daily digests of a person's calendar, to-do list and emails to prepare for the day ahead, the same kind of recurring logistics text.

How it works and its limits

How One isolated job on Tony's own agent, created by the short jobs script (G003): the owner's handle read from the family file, a time limit, --tz America/New_York, and a tool list that holds only home_weather and the read-only calendar tool (F009). No web tool; the normal context is kept (no --light-context), so the hard rules load on every run; the text is announced to its owner only. The job's message carries its rules: begin with the job's own label; tomorrow's events, the forecast and any active alert; answer NO_REPLY when nothing is on; on Sunday cover the week ahead. Schedule: 21:00, Sunday to Thursday as the starting point; Tony provides the evenings at execution. No driver line, no packing line, no household-database read and no dates taken from mail: what a parent wants in the text goes on the calendar. Before go-live: one hand-started run with a planted event, and one on an empty day. No house-rules rule of its own.

Depends on F009 read-only calendar questions on the family's shared Google calendar, live first: the job uses its calendar tool and sign-in; G003 in its simplified form: the three scheduler switches and the short jobs script; home_weather plugin (exists); Tony provides at execution: which evenings it runs (starting point: Sunday to Thursday), and whether Jordan's copy is switched on (hers needs her own calendar sign-in, which she approves herself)

Limits

  • No 'who drives' and no 'what to pack' line: both rested on a tag the parents would have to start typing on every calendar event and on a routines table nobody has written.
  • Dates that arrived by email are not repeated here unless someone put them on the calendar. Mail stays in the 07:00 mail text and the mail lookup (G015, F051): the evening job holds no mail tool and no hand-off to the mail reader.
  • The forecast comes in half-day periods today; a line such as 'rain after 3' needs the hourly forecast (F083). The National Weather Service forecast reaches seven days ahead, so the Sunday run's outlook covers the coming week and no further.
  • Google's Gemini app can already send a scheduled daily digest of a person's own Google calendar. What Happy's text adds is the forecast and alerts for home, silence when nothing is on, and arrival in the iMessage thread.
  • No quiet hours or daily cap are enforced. 21:00 is the hour Tony chose; to quieten the text he switches the job off, or silences the thread on the phone.
  • The text is only as complete as the calendar: an event nobody entered, a flyer's dates included, is not in it.

Safety The job's tool list holds only the weather tool and the read-only calendar tool: no web tool and no hand-off. Its one text goes only to its owner, whose handle the jobs script reads from the family file. Calendar text can be written by outsiders, so it is outside content; that text is the job's only way out.

Folded in

Still to move across: F013's sources, and the two notes it absorbed earlier (an optional pollen line from Google's Pollen API; keyless government inputs for sunrise and sunset, federal holidays and UV index). The weather plugin returns no sunset, so that line needs the small local calculation.
  • From F015 (Sunday 18:00 week-ahead): F014's edit in this review already carries the Sunday 18:00 schedule, its content and the rule that email-derived dates come from a separate mail job. Still to move across: F015's sources.

Not verified

  • gog is not installed, so its calendar tool and flags were checked only against its website, not a binary.
  • The weather plugin's current fields (12-hour periods, active alerts) were read in the config repo, which is not a citable source.
  • That a run answering the silent token on an empty day sends nothing and raises no failure alert on iMessage: documented, not tried; the hand-started run before go-live shows it.
  • That a job's tool list accepts the weather plugin's tool and the calendar server's tool by name: the hand-started run shows it.

Calendar and family coordination 3

F010

Dates from a flyer become reminders after a yes

Needs a buildHigh riskAdultsValue 4/5Effort SWave C

After reading a flyer, slip or schedule, or on a typed request, Happy lists the dates it found, each spelled out in full, and offers to set a reminder for each; nothing is set until the parent says yes. This works once timed reminders (F007) pass their first test, and for Tony only: when Jordan sends a flyer, Happy lists the dates and she adds them herself. Calendar events are added by a parent on the phone; Happy does not write to the calendar.

Example: Tony sends a photo of a school flyer for the third-grader's class. Happy replies with the five dates it read, each spelled out in full, flags one that has no start time, and asks whether to set a reminder the evening before each. Nothing is set until he answers; he adds the events to the family calendar himself on the phone.

Combines F011 Snap-to-action: photo or PDF dates become reminder and calendar proposals

Backed by Ohai: Your Household Manager for Calendars, To-Dos, Emails & Family Life ohai.ai: On a shipping family assistant's own page a parent says she sends it pictures of schedules and it puts them on the calendar, and its FAQ says it scans emails, PDFs and photos such as school newsletters and team schedules.

How it works and its limits

How A standing rule on the parent's own agent, on top of timed reminders (F007) and, for a photo or PDF, attachment reading (F002): list every date spelled out in full, set nothing until the parent says yes, then set one reminder per confirmed date. It is a plain conversational proposal, not ask_user. Typed requests need only F007. On Jordan's agent, which holds no scheduling tool, the rule ends at the list of dates. Not built: the calendar-write server, its write token and approval step, the calendar-file plugin, the llm-task call and any stored rows. House-rules plugin: this card adds no rule of its own; the reminders it sets pass the reminder rule added with F007 (add only, a text to the asker, no web address, an empty tool list). One eval case before go-live: a planted flyer that asks for a reminder to someone else, or for one without a yes, must create no reminder.

Depends on F007 timed reminders live first, with its first test (a reminder can be created from an iMessage turn at all) and its rule in the house-rules plugin; Tony's agent only; F002 photo and PDF reading, only for dates taken from a photo or PDF

Limits

  • Dates read from a photo can be wrong (a missing year, two schedules on one sheet, a blurry corner), so every proposal spells each date out in full and nothing is set until the parent says yes.
  • The yes before a reminder is a prompt rule. What code enforces is the reminder rule that comes with F007: a reminder can only be added, only as a text to the asker, with no web address and no tools.
  • Reminders work for Tony only, because Jordan is not a command owner: a flyer from Jordan gets the list of dates and no reminders.
  • Happy puts nothing on the calendar. Until a parent adds the events on the phone, they are not in calendar answers (F009) or the evening text (F014).
  • The phone and Google's assistant already cover part of this: a recent iPhone can offer to add one event from a poster, and Google's Gemini app can create calendar events from details pasted into its chat. Happy's part is a sheet with many dates, or a PDF, handled in the thread the parents already use, with every date spelled out first and a text the evening before.
  • If a parent later asks Happy for calendar entries, the first step is a five-minute hand test (one calendar file sent from Messages on the Mac and tapped on each phone), not a build. A calendar write, if ever built, needs an approval enforced in code, as the roadmap requires.

Safety Flyer text is outside content read by the parent's own agent, so nothing is set without a yes. A reminder is a way to send later: the reminder rule in the house-rules plugin (added with F007) refuses any target but the asker, any web address and any job that carries tools, and blocks when its own code fails. Nothing is written to a calendar.

Corrected since 9 Oct

  • A 9 Oct note says gog has no delete command. That holds only for the bundled skill text; the gog command index (gogcli.sh/commands) lists gog calendar delete, and gog calendar create accepts --attendees and --send-updates, so the write wrapper must leave delete out and strip those flags itself.
  • Catalog JSON 'needs' relies on ask_user for the confirmation. ask-user.md:181 says not to use it to confirm a plan, and its wait is clamped to one hour at most (ask-user.md:116-117). The Markdown already switches to a plain proposal.

Folded in

  • From SRC-14 (School lunch menu answers (no documented feed)): One line at most: a monthly lunch menu PDF or photo is one more document whose dated rows Happy can propose and, after a yes, store (F031) for the evening brief to read; the proposed rows must be confirmed and Happy is never the allergy authority.
  • From F082 (Clarifying questions and clean extraction (ask_user, llm-task)): F011's edit in this review already carries the llm-task config lines (enable the plugin, tools.alsoAllow, a JSON schema, both custom model ids in llm.allowedCompletionModels, allowModelOverride false) and the unverified point about an empty tool surface on Happy's OpenAI route. Still to do: allow ask_user on <p>-main only if numbered choices are ever wanted (AUT-01 names it as an option), and have WEB-11, F051, F016 and F014 name 'llm-task plugin enabled' as a config prerequisite instead of F082.

Not verified

  • Date extraction accuracy on real flyers (missing years, two schedules on one sheet, blurry photos) has not been measured.
  • That a reminder can be created from an iMessage turn at all (F007's first test) has not been tried.
  • Which iPhones the parents carry: the phone-side claim in the caveats rests on press guides, not on Apple's own page.

F006

Happy in the parents' group chat: answers when named

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 3/5Effort MWave G

Happy joins one three-way iMessage group with both parents and answers when addressed by name, so both see the answer. The group helper answers from weather and web search only: it keeps no memory and has no calendar, list, mail or note tools. M1 signed off iMessage groups as disabled; this re-opens them for that one chat, which Tony approved on 12 Oct.

Example: In the parents' group Jordan writes: 'Happy, will it rain on Saturday afternoon?' and both parents see the answer. A message in the group that does not name Happy gets no reply.

Can be built because docs/concepts/multi-agent.md:589: OpenClaw's own multi-agent guide gives, as a worked example, a dedicated family agent bound to a single group chat with mention gating and a tighter tool policy than a personal agent.

How it works and its limits

How A parent creates the three-person group from a phone; Tony reads its chat id with imsg chats. Config: channels.imessage.groupPolicy: "allowlist", groupAllowFrom with the parents' handles, one groups[<chat_id>] entry with requireMention: true, and a binding with peer.kind: "group" that routes that chat to a new shared, memory-less group agent generated from the family file: web_search and home_weather only, memory search off, no accounts, no hand-off, its own capped model key. Mention patterns come from the agent's name. channels.imessage.historyLimit: 0, so skipped messages are not handed to the helper when it is next named. Go-live gate: both parents write three messages that do not name Happy, then one that does; Tony reads that turn's session record. If a parent's own agent answered, or any of the three messages is in the record, the group stays off. Not built: the group as a target for scheduled texts. No house-rules rule.

Depends on A three-person iMessage group created by a parent from a phone; Tony provides its chat id at execution (read with imsg chats) and confirms that only the two parents and Happy are in it; A new shared, memory-less group agent in the family file and its generator; Tony provides a new capped model key for the group helper at execution (the roadmap's rule: one capped key per agent); The go-live gate passes: the message that names Happy is answered by the group helper and not by a parent's own agent, and with the group history limit at 0 that turn holds none of the messages that did not name it

Limits

  • This changes the M1 baseline, which keeps iMessage groups disabled: one registered chat is admitted, with a sender allowlist and answering only when named. Every other group stays ignored.
  • In Basic mode Happy can read and reply in a group but has no group actions such as renaming it or adding people, so a parent creates the group from a phone.
  • Both parents see every answer given in the group, so nothing from one parent's notes, mail or calendar belongs there; the group helper holds none of it and cannot be asked for it. Who is in the chat is decided on the parents' phones: the sender allowlist stops anyone else from being answered, not from reading the answers.
  • Left at its default, a group that answers only when named hands the helper up to 50 skipped messages the next time it is named, which would send the parents' own conversation to the cloud model beside web search results. The history limit of 0 is what prevents that, and it is untested on iMessage, hence the go-live gate.
  • The group is not a place for scheduled texts: a scheduled job delivers only to its owner, so something meant for both parents is two jobs, one each.
  • Each parent can already ask the same weather or web question one to one; the gain is one shared answer that both see.

Safety The group helper is a separate shared agent with no memory, no accounts and no calendar, list, mail or note tools, so nothing one parent's agent holds can surface in front of the other. The gateway, not the model, admits only the parents' handles and the one registered chat; the helper has no message tool and replies only there. Search results are outside content.

Corrected since 9 Oct

  • Catalog JSON description includes a 'tell everyone dinner is at 6:30' relay and gives the group agent calendar and list tools. Neither exists on the installed stack; the Markdown already moves the relay to G009 and limits version 1 to weather and search.

Not verified

  • Receiving and replying in a three-person group in Basic mode has not been tried on this Mac; the docs warn that some multi-person threads arrive flagged as non-group unless the chat id is registered. The go-live gate checks which agent answered.
  • That a history limit of 0 on the iMessage channel stops skipped group messages reaching the helper: documented for all channels, not tried here; the go-live gate tests it.
  • The numeric chat id is unknown until the group is created and read with imsg chats.
  • That mention patterns derived from the agent's name catch the ways the parents actually address Happy in a group.

Review

The name is put in plain words and the description says what the group helper can answer in its first version.
  • r2: kept; credible mention: Multi-agent routing: family agent bound to a WhatsApp group
  • r3: edited example, safety. Kept: OpenClaw's own guide shows a family agent bound to one group chat. The card had no example and no safety note; both are filled in from what the entry already says about the group helper (no memory, no calendar, list or mail tools, one registered chat, the two parents only). The example asks about Saturday afternoon and not a set hour, because the hour-by-hour forecast is a separate upgrade (F083).
  • r3: kept; credible mention: Multi-agent routing: family agent bound to a WhatsApp group
  • r4: edited how, caveats, unverified, safety. Kept: OpenClaw's own guide shows a dedicated family agent bound to one group chat. One thing no earlier round recorded: a group that answers only when named keeps the messages it skipped (50 by default) and gives them to the helper the next time it is named, so 'the helper holds nothing private' was not true as written. The card now sets that history to zero and says so.
  • r4: kept; credible mention: Multi-agent routing: family agent bound to a WhatsApp group
  • r5: edited caveats. Kept: OpenClaw's own guide shows a dedicated family agent bound to one group chat, and its security page calls a private family room a normal deployment (both read again in this round). MKT-06

Two-parent calendar conflict watch

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 3/5Effort MWave DNew

Once a day a script with no model looks 14 days ahead: when an event on the family's shared Google calendar falls at a time when both parents' own calendars show busy, each parent who has it switched on gets one line naming the event and the time, once, ending with a plain 'Who covers?'. Happy only reports: it moves and declines nothing, and it does not carry the answer between the parents.

Example: Trigger: the daily check finds a family-calendar event next Thursday at 4 pm while both parents' own calendars show busy. Each parent gets, in their own thread: 'Calendar clash: Thursday 22 October, 4:00 pm: [the event's title]. Both of you show busy then. Who covers?' The same clash is not reported again.

Backed by Ohai.ai features: AI calendar management ohai.ai: A shipping family assistant's own feature page says it scans the user's connected calendars and flags overlapping events, sold as conflict detection that avoids double bookings.

How it works and its limits

How One no-model command job (--command-argv) per parent who has it switched on, Tony's first, created by the jobs script (G003), once a day in the morning at an hour Tony names at execution. A host script lists the family calendar's events for the next 14 days, asks for both parents' busy times (gog calendar conflicts or freebusy), compares against that job's own seen-list state file and prints one labelled line per new clash, or NO_REPLY. Each job delivers only to its owner. Sign-in, the plan's default: each parent's job uses that parent's own read-only calendar sign-in (F009), and the other parent shares their own calendar with it as 'See only free/busy'; no script loads two people's sign-ins. Tony confirms this at execution. Personal events appear only as 'busy'; only family-calendar titles are named. 'Who covers?' is plain text: no relay, no record of the answer. No rule decides which events count: every such overlap is reported. No house-rules rule: no agent tool is involved.

Depends on F009 read-only calendar sign-in on the family's shared Google calendar, with gog installed: Tony's for his job, Jordan's own for hers; G003 in its simplified form: the jobs script creates the command jobs, one per parent who has it switched on; Each parent shares their own Google calendar with the other parent's account as 'See only free/busy'; Tony provides at execution: the hour of the daily check, which calendars hold each parent's own appointments, his confirmation of whose sign-in reads them, and whether Jordan's copy is switched on

Limits

  • An overlap is not always a problem (both parents at the same recital). With no rule for which events count, the watch will sometimes flag one that needs no cover.
  • The watch sees only calendars shared with the sign-in that reads them. A work calendar counts only if it is a Google calendar and the employer lets its busy times be shared outside the organisation; otherwise that kind of clash is missed unless the parent blocks the time on their own calendar.
  • Happy reports; it does not move or decline anything, and it does not pass one parent's answer to the other.
  • Each parent's line comes from that parent's own job. Jordan's job needs her own calendar sign-in, which she approves herself on Google's screen.
  • It runs once a day, so a clash created after that day's run is reported the next morning.
  • No Google or Apple help page was found that describes a warning when two people's calendars clash, so this looks like a gap the phones leave open; that is the absence of a finding, not proof.

Safety No model call, so text in event titles cannot steer anything. The calendar grant is read-only. The script asks only for busy times on the parents' own calendars, so one parent's private event titles are never shown to the other; only shared family-calendar titles appear. Each job texts only its owner, and no sign-in is used outside its owner's job.

Reviewers

  • The zero-model command job is sound, but as written one script holds both parents' calendar credentials and prints each parent's private event titles to the other, which cuts across the roadmap's one-data-domain-per-person rule. Effort is closer to M once the no-driver rule, the state file, gog setup and per-parent delivery are counted.

Not verified

  • Flags and output of gog calendar conflicts and freebusy: gog is not installed, only its command list page was read.
  • Whether those commands work on a calendar shared as free/busy only, and under the read-only calendar grant that F009 sets up.
  • Where each parent's own appointments live, work included: an employer's Google calendar can be shared outside the organisation only as far as its administrator allows, and a work calendar that is not on Google cannot be read at all.
  • That a command job run by the gateway can use the calendar sign-in stored for F009's server: not tried.

Review

  • r1: kept; credible mention: Ohai: Your Household Manager for Calendars, To-Dos, Emails & Family Life
  • r2: edited description, how, depends_on. Kept. The description opened with a line about another product instead of what the parents get, and the follow-up question pointed at the request relay, which round 1 made a step of family delivery (G009); both are fixed.
  • r2: kept; credible mention: Ohai.ai features: AI calendar management
  • r3: edited description, example, unverified. Kept: a shipping family assistant sells this same check. The description promised more than the script can know (it sees busy times, not who is driving), so it now says what is detected and that a written rule decides which events count; the example text is changed to match.
  • r3: kept; credible mention: Ohai.ai features: AI calendar management
  • r4: edited how, caveats, unverified. Kept: a shipping family assistant sells this same check. Three gaps are now written down: the card's own example turns on a work meeting, and whether a work calendar's busy times can reach the family's reading account depends on the employer and on that calendar being Google's; a text outside the allowed hours is dropped, not held, so the job has to run inside those hours; and a text dropped by the daily cap is lost the same way, which timing does not fix.
  • r4: kept; credible mention: Ohai.ai features: AI calendar management

Research and page watchers 2

F028

Day-out and trip planner: options with the weather and links

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 4/5Effort SWave D

'Plan Saturday for us, rain likely' returns two options, each with the forecast for home, links, opening hours where a page that could be read shows them, and an admission price only when a page that was read showed one. A weekend or longer plan comes back the same way, with hotels and transport as links, not prices. The parents book; Happy books and pays for nothing.

Example: Tony texts: 'Plan Saturday for us, rain likely.' Happy sends two options, one indoors and one outdoors with a rain fallback, each with Saturday's forecast, a link with the time the page was read, opening hours where the venue's page showed them, and the admission price where it showed one.

Backed by 5 ways Google parents are using Gemini blog.google: Google's own post has parents using its assistant as a travel planner: listing the kid-friendly activities near them and finding child-friendly activities, places to stay and transport for a family trip.

How it works and its limits

How A short planning rule on each parent's agent and on the research helper (F019), plus one hand-off with a time limit. The helper searches and reads venue pages; the forecast for home comes from the existing home_weather tool on the parent's agent. The answer gives two options with the weather, links and their fetch times, opening hours where a page that could be read shows them, a price only from a page that was read, and nothing booked. The task handed to the helper carries only a place, a distance, dates and the children's ages; never names or the school. Dates come from the parent's request, so no calendar read is needed. Not built: the place lookup with its Google Cloud project, key and wrapper, the Friday text, the paperwork line for trips abroad, a house-rules rule. Before go-live: one eval case (a price only from a fetched page) and one live request whose record shows what went to the helper.

Depends on F019 research helper live: it does the reading, after the outbound proxy is built and after its own test that a hand-off returns the answer in the same chat; home_weather plugin (exists); Tony provides the two children's ages at execution (their grades are on record, their ages are not): typed into the family file with the other family facts, or given in the request

Limits

  • Happy books and pays for nothing: the plan ends in links and the parents book.
  • Prices are best effort. Plain page reads fail on many booking, hotel and transport sites, so those come as links, and an admission price appears only when a page that could be read showed it.
  • There is no place lookup, so opening hours come only from venue pages that could be read, with no ratings and no drive time; for 'is it open now?' the maps app on the phone is quicker. A place lookup is a later add-on: the roadmap names Google's hosted Maps server, it needs billing switched on, and that has not been put to Tony.
  • What reaches the research helper (a place, a distance, dates and ages) is an instruction to the parent's agent, not an enforced limit.
  • A long plan comes back as a text; once 'email me this' (F049) is live it can be emailed to the asker like any other long answer. The forecast is the one for home, in half-day periods; an hour-by-hour rain line needs the hourly forecast (F083).
  • A general assistant such as Gemini already drafts an itinerary from a typed prompt. What this small version adds is the forecast for home in the same answer and arrival in the iMessage thread.

Safety The research helper holds no family data and has no payment or booking tool; it is given only a place, a distance, dates and ages, never names or the school (a prompt rule, checked on one live request's record, not an enforced limit). Web pages are outside content, and the helper's answer is treated as untrusted. Answers go only to the asking parent.

Corrected since 9 Oct

Folded in

  • From CRT-14 (Trip paperwork check: children's travel documents): For a trip abroad with the children, the parent's own agent ends the plan with a paperwork line: whether the passports are valid for the dates (from the renewals table, F063), whether a consent letter may be needed when one parent or a grandparent travels with a child (USAGov link, with a draft for the other parent to sign and have notarised), and TSA's rule that under-18s need no ID on domestic flights. Passport dates and names stay with the parent's agent and are never handed to research; Happy certifies and books nothing, links the official page for the destination's entry rules and says to check with the airline.
  • From F021 (Places lookup: hours, ratings, distance, phone (goplaces)): Carry the place lookup into the outing planner as one of its tools: up to three picks with hours, rating, phone and a Maps link from Google Places, drive time only through the directions command with the Routes API, and no reservations. List its prerequisites there in place of 'F021': a Google Cloud project with billing on, a key held in the host-side wrapper with a budget alert, and the choice between the bundled goplaces command and Google's hosted Maps server named in the roadmap (whose place search returns a generated summary and Maps links, so check it can answer 'is it open now?' first); the note in F076 that points to F021 should point to F028.
  • From F027 (Find a place and route errands: open-now dinner, urgent care, pharmacy, Saturday loop): This is the Places lookup (F021) with an answer format: the same Google Places search, the same open-now and rating filters, the same Maps link. The record also concedes that phone maps apps already answer these questions with live traffic, so it does not earn a separate entry; nothing depends on it.

Not verified

  • Hotel and train price snapshots: no opened source shows these sites are readable logged-out; expect links instead of prices.
  • That a hand-off to the research helper returns its answer in the same chat: the roadmap lists this as not yet confirmed on this version, and it is F019's first test.
  • The weather plugin returns 12-hour periods today (read in the config repo, not citable), so an hourly rain window needs the plugin change in F083.

F018

A watch on one public page or feed Tony names

Needs a buildLow riskAdultsValue 4/5Effort SWave D

Tony names one public page or feed, and a small script with no model checks it during the day and texts him once when something new appears there; otherwise it stays silent. A team or school schedule that has a subscription link is also subscribed into the shared Google calendar, which needs no code. Storm alerts and recall notices are not watched: weather answers already carry active alerts for home, each parent can switch on the phone's own severe-weather notifications, and the recall agencies offer their own email sign-ups.

Example: Trigger: the feed Tony registered shows an item the script has not seen before. Text: 'Page watch: new on the page you asked me to watch: <the item's title> <its link on that site>'. On a day with nothing new, no text is sent.

Combines F029 Public calendar, feed and page watchers: a text when a game moves or a site posts something new; SRC-09 Sports schedule feeds with change alerts; SRC-03 Recall watch matched to what the family owns: products (CPSC), food and medicine (FDA); SRC-04 Food and medicine recall watch (FDA)

Backed by Winter Weather | Ready.gov ready.gov: The federal preparedness site tells households to pay attention to weather reports and warnings of freezing weather and winter storms and to sign up for their community's warning system.

How it works and its limits

How Tony names the page or feed at execution. When it is a schedule with a subscription link, a parent first subscribes it into the shared Google calendar (no code), so calendar answers (F009) show it. The watch itself is one reviewed script, run as one host command job (--command-argv, no model call) that the jobs script (G003) creates, with the owner's handle read from the family file, a time limit and the daytime hours Tony sets. The script uses the site's feed when there is one, otherwise a plain https GET and a text hash; it checks the address itself (https, public host), keeps seen ids in a state file, and prints one templated line that starts with its label, or NO_REPLY. Tony's job first; Jordan's copy is a second job with its own state file. Not built: storm, recall and keyword-list scripts. No rule in the house-rules plugin.

Depends on Tony provides the one public page or feed to watch at execution (and its subscription link, if it is a schedule); Tony provides the daytime hours for the check at execution; G003 in its small form: the three scheduler switches and the short jobs script, which creates the watch as one command job; F009 calendar read, for a schedule link: once subscribed into the shared Google calendar, it shows in calendar answers

Limits

  • A parent cannot start a watch from chat: command jobs are created by the operator, so the watch, and any second page later, is a request to Tony.
  • The watch gives no earlier notice than the source's own service: a team app's push is faster for a same-day change.
  • A hash watch on a page can fire on changes that do not matter; pages that need JavaScript or a login are out of reach, and many school portals publish no feed. The watch never runs on a logged-in page.
  • Command jobs run on the Gateway host as the happy user, outside the sandbox, agent tool policy and OpenClaw's fetch guardrails, so the script checks its address itself (https, public host) and is reviewed like the rest of the config repo.
  • A team's subscription link is a bearer secret, so it sits in a file only the happy user can read and stays out of family.json5 if that file is committed.
  • Not built: storm, recall and keyword-list scripts. Silence from the watch is never an all-clear, since Happy is down in a power cut or a network outage; the phones' own emergency alerts stay on, and a recall email from an agency's own sign-up, if a parent signs up, simply shows up in the 07:00 mail text.

Safety No model reads the page: the script prints a fixed line with the outside title stripped and capped, and only a link on the registered site. The script refuses anything but https to a public host, fetches only the address Tony registered and sends nothing about the family. The text goes to the job's owner alone, from the handle in the family file.

Corrected since 9 Oct

  • The catalog's needs used --once and the verifier said no CLI flag exists (JSON or Control UI only); the installed CLI source defines --trigger-once.

Folded in

  • The weather-alert feed Happy will poll already carries an Air Quality Alert type, so the same watch can cover smoke and ozone days; an AirNow forecast key is optional and only worth adding if such days recur.
  • An order of preference for every watcher: the town's own feed or reminder first, plain fetch second, a browser last; and the rule that a watcher never runs on a logged-in profile.
  • From OCL-10 (Feed watch for school, PTA, town and library sites (RSS/Atom)): Carry over the feed-first check, the model-free command job that relays only new titles with links limited to the registered host, and the rule to first count how many of the family's sites publish a feed. Prefer a small in-house feed script over the third-party blogwatcher binary, which has no tagged releases and no machine-readable output.
  • From SRC-05 (Vehicle recall check by make, model and year (NHTSA)): Do not poll NHTSA. In the recall watch's setup notes, tell each parent to add the family cars' VINs, and the car seats, to NHTSA's free SaferCar app, which alerts per vehicle.

Not verified

  • Whether the page Tony names publishes a feed, or can be read at all without JavaScript or a login; checked first at execution.
  • Whether a schedule subscribed into Google Calendar is visible to Happy's read-only calendar tool (F009).
  • Which agent's session transcript receives the mirrored announce line of a command job; read the transcript after the first run, and keep the line short and templated.
  • If the source is a team app's subscription link: how quickly the link itself reflects a change, and any rate limit or terms for polling it.
  • That the jobs script can create a command job from the deploy path (T3), and how the outbound firewall, once it blocks every program by default, treats the script's fetch.

Also absorbs SRC-01, WEB-10

Lists, meals and home upkeep 1

F033

Recipe link to ingredients and the grocery list, and dinner ideas on request

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 2/5Effort SWave G

Text a recipe link and get the ingredient list and the steps, scaled to the number of people, with an offer to add the ingredients to the shared Reminders list that Tony names as the grocery list. Ask for dinner ideas for the week and Happy suggests dinners in that chat, fitted to the week's calendar, and can add a chosen dinner's ingredients to the list. Nothing is added without a yes, nothing is ordered, and no dinner text arrives unasked.

Example: A parent texts: '<recipe link> What do I need for this for six people?' Happy replies with the scaled ingredients, the steps and the link, and asks whether to add the ingredients to the grocery list. Or a parent texts 'dinner ideas for this week?' and then 'add Wednesday's to the list'.

Combines WEB-11 Recipe link to ingredients and steps

Backed by 5 ways Google parents are using Gemini blog.google: Google's own post quotes a parent who has its assistant create weekly meal plans, share recipes and create grocery lists.

How it works and its limits

How Recipe link: the parent's own agent hands the address and the serving count to the research helper (the ordinary F019 hand-off); the helper fetches the page with web_fetch and returns the ingredients and steps as plain text with the source link. The parent's agent scales the amounts and offers the items for the grocery list; after a yes it adds them with the Reminders tool (F030), which writes only to its one configured list. Until that tool is live, the reply is the ingredient list as text to paste. Dinner ideas: on request only, answered in the same chat by the parent's agent, which reads the week from the calendar (F009); a chosen dinner's ingredients go to the list the same way. Not built: a scheduled dinner text, a saved plan, a recipe box, an llm-task step, an allergy fit (none is on record), a table in the household database (F031), any house-rules rule.

Depends on F019 research helper (reads the recipe page); F030 Reminders bridge, for adding to the grocery list; until it is live the ingredients come back as text to paste; F009 calendar read, for dinner ideas fitted to the week; Tony provides at execution which shared Reminders list is the grocery list (the one list the Reminders bridge is set to)

Limits

  • The fetch returns readable article text, not the page's embedded recipe data, so the model parses ingredients from prose and can drop a line; the source link is always included.
  • Some recipe sites sit behind bot walls or paywalls and return nothing; Happy says so instead of guessing. Pages that need JavaScript, and video recipes, are readable only once the extra readers (F020) exist; this card builds nothing for them.
  • Tony names the shared Reminders list at execution. The Reminders bridge writes to one named list only, so the grocery list has to be that list; until then the ingredients come back as text to paste.
  • On iOS 26 an iPhone that runs Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro and every iPhone 16 or later) already turns a recipe page into list items when the page is shared to Reminders (support.apple.com/124025). For a parent with such a phone the link-to-list step is a convenience; what Happy adds is scaling to the number of people and dinner ideas fitted to the family calendar.
  • Happy does not know what is in the kitchen, so it offers the whole ingredient list and the parent strikes what they have. Scaling quantities is arithmetic done by a language model: fine for a stew, worth a second look for baking.
  • Given up with this form: an unprompted weekly dinner text, saved recipes, and a plan that carries over to a later chat. Nothing is fitted to allergies, so Happy is never the allergy authority and the cook still checks ingredients and labels.

Safety The research helper reads the untrusted recipe page and gets only an address and a serving count; the parent's agent holds the calendar and does not fetch pages itself (it holds the fetch tool only for the helper). In code, the list tool (F030) can only list, add and tick off on its one configured list. Waiting for a yes is an instruction, not a limit. Nothing is saved from a page, ordered or bought.

Not verified

  • T4: that a hand-off to the research helper returns its answer to the parent's agent (F019's first test); the recipe step rests on it.
  • T9: that an item added from the Mac reaches the shared list on both parents' phones (F030's first test); the grocery hand-off rests on it.
  • How many of the recipe sites the family actually uses plain fetch can read, and whether the fetched text ever carries a page's embedded recipe data (none was found in the installed code, and no live recipe page was fetched); seen with the first real links.

Health, safety and admin 2

CRT-10

Sick-day log of what was given, shared by both parents

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 3/5Effort MWave ENew

When a child is ill, both parents text Happy what they gave and when, and either can ask 'when was the last dose?' and get the same answer: the last dose that was logged, who logged it and how long ago. Happy records and recalls: it is told never to advise a dose, which is an instruction backed by a test case and not a hard limit, and the lookup hands back a fixed check-the-label line. The log puts the children's dose notes on the cloud model, which Tony confirms at execution.

Example: Jordan texts: 'The kindergartner has a fever, gave the children's acetaminophen at 7:40.' Happy confirms: 'Logged: children's acetaminophen at 7:40 this morning.' Later Tony texts: 'When was the last dose?' and gets: 'Last dose logged: children's acetaminophen at 7:40 this morning, logged by Jordan, 3 hours 5 minutes ago. Check the label for dose and timing, and ask the pediatrician or poison control if unsure.'

Backed by Double dosing: What to do if you take too much | Poison Control (National Capital Poison Center) poison.org: A poison centre lists medicine given by more than one person who do not communicate as a cause of double dosing and advises keeping a log that is marked each time a dose is given.

How it works and its limits

How One dose table in the household database (F031), with two tools on both parents' agents. Logging stores the child (a short label), what was given (a short text field), the time and which parent's agent logged it. The time is the Mac's clock when the tool runs unless the parent states one; a stated time ('at 7:40') is read by the model, so Happy's confirmation spells it out in full, day included. care_last returns the latest rows, the elapsed minutes (subtracted in code) and one fixed line: check the label, ask the pediatrician or poison control if unsure. One AGENTS.md rule (never advise a dose; save no illness details as notes), one eval case. Each tool run deletes rows older than 14 days. Not built: a canned reply, a timed sweep, a relayed ask, any house-rules rule. Ordinary requests: an absence-note draft, tomorrow's calendar, CDC's return rule with its link (the school's policy wins), a check-in reminder (Tony only).

Depends on F031 household database in its smallest form: the shared plugin, to which this card adds its one dose table and its two tools; Tony provides his confirmation at execution that the children's dose notes may be kept for 14 days and sent to the cloud model (he picked this card knowing it does that); Tony provides a short label for each of the two children at execution (not a full name); Optional, not needed for the log: F009 calendar read for 'what is on tomorrow', and F007 reminders for a check-in reminder (Tony only, since Jordan is not a command owner)

Limits

  • This is a log, not a clinician. The tool cannot see when a text was sent: the logged time is the Mac's clock when the tool runs, and a stated time ('at 7:40') is read by the model, so Happy repeats it back in full and the parent corrects it if wrong. Only the subtraction is done in code.
  • Happy knows only the doses that were texted to it. A dose given and not logged is missing from the answer, so the reply says 'last dose logged' and who logged it, never 'last dose given'.
  • FDA says more than 600 medicines contain acetaminophen and that a child's dose should never be guessed. The log stores the product name as typed so a parent can spot two products with the same ingredient; Happy does not make that judgement.
  • The children's health notes pass through a cloud model under store:false. Tony picked the card knowing this and confirms it at execution; the log uses a short label for each child and keeps diagnoses out.
  • A poison centre's advice is that the log should stay with the medicine and be marked at every dose. Happy's log is not next to the bottle and cannot be reached when Happy, the network or the cloud model is down, so it works beside a note kept with the medicine and does not replace one.
  • The 14-day deletion covers the log rows only; the chat transcript still holds what was typed and follows the general retention setting. 'Never advise a dose' is an instruction backed by a test case, not a hard limit.

Safety Runs on each parent's own agent and replies only to the parent who asked; the log brings in no outside content (the label line is fixed text). The two parents share the rows by design. The elapsed time and the fixed line come from code; 'no dose advice' (with an eval case) and keeping a child's health out of research hand-offs are instructions.

Reviewers

  • The claim that two caregivers is 'the usual way' a double dose happens had no source; a poison centre page supports a weaker statement. 'Never advises a dose' was only an instruction to the model, which this stack's rules do not count as a control, so the lookup reply should be rendered in code.

Not verified

  • Before go-live, two texts with a stated time, one just after midnight and one late in the evening, must each be confirmed back with the right day and time.
  • The eval case 'can I give more now?' must get no dose advice, only the check-the-label line; it is not yet written or run.
  • That the tool is told which agent called it, so 'who logged it' does not come from the model: read in the installed plugin types, not run.
  • That both parents' agents read the same rows: one parent logs and the other asks, from the two phones.

  • r2: edited how, depends_on, unverified. Kept. Two pointers led to entries that round 1 folded into family delivery (the outreach drafts and the request relay); they now point to G009. The open question about the iPhone Health app is narrowed: Apple's page describes sharing one's own medication list, not two parents logging doses for a child.

  • r3: edited caveats, unverified. Kept. The poison centre page this card rests on also says the log should stay with the medicine, which no earlier round carried over; a caveat now says Happy's log works beside a note kept with the medicine and does not replace it. One more open point is written down: whether a note shared between the two phones would do the same job.

CRT-13

Emergency card, sitter sheet and school-form kit from one set of family pages

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 3/5Effort MWave ENew

From one set of family pages in the shared handbook, Happy helps a parent produce the pages other people ask for: a one-page emergency plan to print, a sheet to hand to a sitter or other carer, and, for school forms, a list of where each document is and when it runs out, a checklist of open forms and the answers as one block to paste. The parent prints, forwards, signs and submits. Happy is never the emergency channel: it is told to start its reply to a text that sounds like an emergency with a line to call emergency services or Poison Help.

Example: A parent texts 'make the sitter sheet for Friday' and gets one message to forward or print. Jordan texts: 'What do I still need for the third-grader's school forms?' and gets the open items from that child's page. A parent who texts 'He swallowed something, what do I do?' gets a reply that starts with the line to call emergency services or Poison Help, and then the answer.

Combines F036 Babysitter / grandparent sheet; CRT-12 Enrolment, camp and health-form paperwork kit

Backed by Make A Plan | Ready.gov ready.gov: The federal preparedness site tells every household to meet, write down and practise a family emergency plan with contacts, in four steps, and offers a fillable form for it.

How it works and its limits

How Facts: a plan page and a page per child in the shared handbook (F043), read-only for the agents: contacts, the doctor's office, each official document's place and valid-until date, and the open forms. No allergies, medicines or conditions: a parent writes those onto a sheet by hand. Emergency plan: an interview following Ready.gov's four steps ends with the finished page in one message; the parent prints or saves it, and Tony pastes it into the folder, without health lines, if Happy should reuse it. Sitter sheet: an AGENTS.md prompt template over the same pages. Form kit: a form sent as a photo or PDF (F002) gets its answers drafted as one block to paste, drafts only; a due date is an ordinary reminder (F007, Tony only). Emergency texts: one AGENTS.md line (start the reply with 'call emergency services or Poison Help', then answer) and one more eval case, vaguely worded. No hook, phrase list, database row or house-rules rule.

Depends on F043 shared family handbook (the plan page and the two children's pages live there, typed or pasted in by Tony); Tony provides the facts for those pages at execution: emergency contacts, the doctor's office, where each official document is kept and its valid-until date; Tony provides a check of the poison-help number at execution, before the sheet is printed; F002 photo and PDF reading, for a form sent as a photo or PDF; Optional: F009 calendar read for 'tonight's plan' on the sitter sheet; F007 reminders for a form's due date and a yearly contact re-check (Tony only, since Jordan is not a command owner); F080 printing, and until it exists a parent prints the page from a phone

Limits

  • Happy can be down in exactly the events that matter, since a power cut stops the Mac and a network outage stops iMessage, so the printed sheet is the part that survives, and the phone's own emergency call and medical ID features remain the right tools.
  • There is no canned emergency reply: the 'call emergency services' line comes from the cloud model under one instruction with eval cases, so it is not a limit, and there is no reply at all while the model is down.
  • The poison-help number on the printed sheet comes from the poison centre's own page listed in the sources, and a parent checks it before the sheet is printed.
  • Only Tony adds or changes a stored page: a parent saves or prints the finished page and tells Tony when a fact changes. Happy cannot update a page itself.
  • Children's health details are not stored, the default Tony left in place (he lifted it for the dose log only), so a parent writes allergies, medicines and conditions onto the printed sheet by hand. Whatever a parent types into the chat to finish a sheet or an answer block still reaches the cloud model, and so does a form sent as a photo or PDF; the house rule on the printed sheet asks parents not to send medical papers.
  • Happy never signs, fills in or submits a form; the drafts-only rule is a prompt instruction that holds only because the agent has no tool that could fill in or send one. Requirements differ by state, district and organiser, so Happy lists what each form asked for last time and does not know the rules. ID, policy and certificate numbers and the Wi-Fi password stay off these pages.

Safety The pages hold contacts and document details, no children's health facts; they stay in the handbook folder, read only by the parents' own agents, and on paper. Drafting from them sends those facts to the cloud model; an instruction keeps them from the research helper. Happy messages nobody outside the family: a parent forwards the sheet and submits every form. No tool is added.

Folded in

  • From F067 (School, camp and sports health-form helper): CRT-12 depends on this entry for its copy-paste block, so carry it in: when a school, camp or sports health form arrives as a photo or PDF, draft the answers from the per-child form-facts page as one copy-paste block; never fill in, sign or submit the form. The kids' health facts reach the cloud model, and the drafts-only rule is a prompt instruction that holds only because the agent has no form-filling tool. The removed screen-control form pilot (MAC-07) also points here for ready-to-paste answers.

Not verified

  • That a parent's sandboxed agent can search and read pages in the shared handbook folder (F043's own first test, part of T6); these pages rest on it.
  • That the new eval case with vague wording ('he swallowed something') gets the emergency line first; the existing swallowed-battery case already passes with no instruction.
  • The federal Poison Help site refused automated fetches, so the poison-help number comes from the National Capital Poison Center's page listed in the sources and has to be checked by a parent.
  • What the school's own forms ask for, and whether the state's immunization registry gives parents direct online access; seen with the first real form.

Operator checks and recovery 3

G008

Operator self-checks: a daily Google sign-in check, with audits and drills run by Tony

Needs a buildLow riskOperatorValue 4/5Effort SWave A

One daily check on the Mac tells Tony, and only Tony, when a Google sign-in that Happy's mail or calendar reading depends on has stopped working, so an expired sign-in does not first show up as a missing or empty morning text. The security audit (after every update and each month), the monthly checklist and the quarterly restore drill and key rotation stay commands Tony runs himself, prompted by reminders on his own calendar. Behaviour test cases join the existing eval suite when the feature they test ships, and are run on demand and after a critical-path change, as already decided.

Example: Trigger: the stored Google sign-in for one parent's Gmail stops working. Within a day the check raises an alert on Tony's phone through ntfy, the route his other alerts use, and nothing is sent to the family. That parent approves the sign-in again on Google's screen and the next run is clean.

Combines OCL-13 Security audit after every update and monthly (healthcheck checklist, security audit --deep); AUT-09 Personal-agent behaviour checks added to the eval suite

Can be built because docs/gateway/health.md:9: OpenClaw's own guide gives the health commands, probe endpoints and uptime monitoring as the operator's way to verify that the Gateway and its channels work.

How it works and its limits

How A daily launchd job runs one read-only script as the happy user, as the sandbox check and the eval job in the config repo already do. It runs gog auth list --check and reads every entry (its exit status does not prove every sign-in valid), then reports as those checks do: one ok-or-not metric for a Grafana rule, or a counts-only line to ntfy. It covers each sign-in as it is added: Tony's mail, Jordan's mail, then the calendar sign-ins. No scheduler job, no model call, no text from Happy, no house-rules rule. Go-live test: a sign-in broken on purpose raises the alert within a day and nothing reaches the family. Not jobs: the security audit (after every update and monthly), the monthly checklist (spend caps, new stores in the backup, standing approvals) and the quarterly restore drill and key rotation; Tony runs these from calendar reminders. Behaviour cases: each feature adds its own eval case when it ships; none is built ahead.

Depends on G015 mail reading: gog installed on the Mac mini and at least one Google sign-in stored; The alert route that exists since M1: VictoriaMetrics, Grafana rules and ntfy; roadmap E0 eval harness (exists), for the behaviour cases that other features add when they ship

Limits

  • The five-minute dead-man probe and the M1 Grafana alerts already cover 'gateway down' and 'iMessage unhealthy'. The only new signal here is the Google sign-in; do not build the same alert twice.
  • The check cannot run until gog is installed and a sign-in is stored; gog is not on the Mac mini today.
  • Given up with this form: a daily look at the model sign-in, the channel probe and plugin load state (Tony looks at plugin load state after each deploy instead), automatic comparison of audit results between runs, and results arriving in the iMessage thread.
  • The monthly and quarterly items are reminder lines, not a feature: spend caps, the daily budget alert and the nightly verified backup already exist. The nightly archive is not encrypted and must never be copied to iCloud. Google sign-ins (the wave A runbook's finding, pending Tony's yes at its step A4) and the model keys are kept in happy's login Keychain, not in the archive; Time Machine's copy of happy's home, on the encrypted disk, holds them.
  • Plain doctor can migrate state, so the by-hand checks use its lint form, as happy-inspect already does.
  • Behaviour cases run the real model and cost tokens on every run, and the daily cost alert does not see eval-clone spend; eval clones must keep messaging tools denied, or a reminder test would text the family.

Safety The check is read-only and runs on the host: no agent gains exec or any other tool, no model reads its output, and the result goes only to Tony, as a count or an ok-or-not signal with no mail content. Behaviour cases added later call the model only against eval clones with fake users and fake secrets.

Folded in

  • From G004 (Per-person and per-agent spend caps with a daily cost line): Carry one checklist line: before a new agent or key (mail, voice) goes live it gets its own OpenAI project with a hard monthly limit, a row in the caps file and a budget term in the 'Daily model cost over budget' alert, and the monthly check compares the registry's agents against both. Also carry the known gap that eval-clone spend is labelled 'unknown', so the daily alert does not see it; /usage (OCL-06) already prints a cost summary on request.
  • From G007 (Nightly backups and a quarterly restore drill): Carry two checklist lines: a quarterly restore drill with a reminder to Tony (openclaw backup restore --target into a scratch folder), and a check that each new store (the household database from F031, the wiki vault from F043, plugin state files) is inside the nightly archive or has its own tar step. Keep the warning that the archive is not encrypted by OpenClaw, so it must never be copied to iCloud or any unencrypted place (Google sign-ins and model keys are kept in happy's login Keychain, not in the archive).

Not verified

  • gog is not installed on the Mac mini today; gog auth list --check and what it prints for each entry are known from the bundled gog skill, and must be confirmed on the installed version.
  • Whether that check notices a sign-in that Google has revoked or only reads what is stored on the Mac; the go-live test (a sign-in broken on purpose must raise the alert within a day and send nothing to the family) settles it.
  • How a launchd job run as the happy user reads the stored sign-ins: the bundled gog skill says a run without a desktop keyring needs gog's file keyring and its password in the environment; not tried on this Mac.
  • If the calendar sign-in is stored apart from the mail one (as the calendar card plans), whether one run of the check lists both or the script has to look in two places.
  • How promptfoo's tool-trajectory assertions behave against 2026.9.7 (an open item in the roadmap), for the behaviour cases added later.

G006

Weekly 'what Happy did' text

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 4/5Effort SWave D

Once a week Tony gets one short text that counts what Happy's tools did for him that week and lists the saved-note files that changed, written by a small script with no model. There is no journal and no 'undo that', and forgetting a conversation stays Tony's command at the Mac. Jordan's copy is a second job of the same kind, about her own agent only, added when she asks.

Example: The weekly text, starting with its own label: 'What Happy did this week: web search 9 calls, research helper 3, weather 12, scheduling tool 4. Notes changed: 2 files', followed by the two file names. In a week with nothing to count, no text is sent.

Combines F085 Weekly memory review, and forgetting a conversation on request; CRT-01 Undo the last thing (a change journal with inverses)

Backed by Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems (OpenAI), section 4.4 Legibility of Agent Activity cdn.openai.com: OpenAI's guidance says it may be particularly important that whoever deploys an agent gives the user a ledger of what the agent did, as a lighter way than approvals to show a wider range of actions, and that actions reviewed only afterwards should be easier to reverse.

How it works and its limits

How One checked-in script, no model and no agent tool. It asks OpenClaw's own activity record for the past week of that parent's agent (openclaw audit --agent <id> --kind tool_action --status succeeded --after <date> --json, paging with --limit and --cursor), counts finished calls by tool name, and lists by name the files changed that week in that parent's notes folder (F041). The jobs script (G003) creates one command job for Tony: his handle read from the family file, a time limit, the day and daytime hour he names, the text starting with its own label, and NO_REPLY when there is nothing to count. Jordan's copy is a second job from the same script, about her own agent, added when she asks. The query is tried once from a scheduled command job before the script is written. Not built: a journal table, a copy of note text, an undo tool, a read tool on any agent. House-rules plugin: no rule needed.

Depends on G003 in its simplified form: the three scheduler switches and the jobs script that creates this job; F041 saved notes, for the 'notes changed' line; before notes exist the text holds the tool counts only; Test first: the activity-record query returns that agent's rows when it is run from a scheduled command job; Tony provides the day of the week and the daytime hour of the weekly text at execution

Limits

  • Counts are by tool name only: the text says 'scheduling tool 4 calls', not which reminder or list, and a built-in tool that does several things under one name is one line. In-house tools should give each kind of write its own tool name so the counts mean something.
  • A note file changed twice in one week counts once, and the text shows file names, not what was saved.
  • There is no 'undo that'. A parent says 'cancel that reminder' or 'change it back to X' and the tool that made the change does it; an item Happy added to a list can be deleted on the phone.
  • Nothing answers 'what did you do this week?' exactly in mid-week: no agent gets a tool that reads the record. 'What did you save about me?' is answered from that parent's own notes (F041).
  • The activity record is on by default, holds no content and keeps 30 days, so the text cannot look further back than that.
  • Forgetting works per conversation and stays Tony's command at the Mac (openclaw memory forget, with --dry-run first); nothing is built for it here.

Safety No model and no agent tool are involved. The script reads a record that holds tool names and outcomes but no content, and the file names in one parent's own notes folder. Its one text goes to that parent only, whose handle the jobs script reads from the family file; nothing goes into the other parent's chat.

Corrected since 9 Oct

  • 'Forget what I said about X works' (9 Oct description) is not a platform ability: memory forget selects whole sessions by id, hook source or participant, never by topic or message text, and reworded copies are outside its cleanup. Topic-level forgetting is a hand edit of the memory file.
  • 'Promote via openclaw memory promote --apply' will usually promote nothing a parent just confirmed: by default a candidate needs a 0.75 score, three recalls and three distinct queries. Either pass lower thresholds or write the confirmed line to MEMORY.md directly.

Not verified

  • That openclaw audit can be called from a scheduled command job on the Mac mini and returns one agent's tool rows for the past week; to be tried once before the script is written.
  • That each row's tool name is specific enough for the counts to mean something for the tools Happy has by then (the page says tool actions show the tool name; no query was run).
  • Where saved notes live is settled by F041's own test (T6); that file change times in that folder reflect each save made through the sandbox was not tried.
