CRT-05

Half page for Jordan: how to tell that Happy is down

Ready nowMedium riskOperatorValue 4/5Effort SWave BNew

Jordan gets one printed half page: how to recognise that Happy is down, that nothing in the house is broken, and who to call. After a power cut Happy stays down until Tony unlocks the Mac at home, as the roadmap row he chose says. There is no envelope, no password on paper and no Terminal step.

Example: A power cut while Tony is out. Happy stops answering, and Jordan reads the half page: no reply within a few minutes means Happy is down, nothing is broken, and it comes back when Tony unlocks the Mac.

Backed by Get to know your Emergency Kit (1Password Support) support.1password.com: A shipping password manager tells customers to print a recovery sheet, keep it somewhere safe and hand a copy to a trusted person such as a spouse, so access survives when the owner is unavailable.

How it works and its limits

How No software, so no house-rules rule. Tony writes and prints a half page for Jordan: (1) how to tell that Happy is down: no reply within a few minutes, or the error line a parent sees when a turn fails, worded from what test T8 showed on his own phone; (2) nothing is broken: after a power cut the Mac waits at the disk-unlock screen and Happy stays down until Tony unlocks it; (3) who to call. Not on the page and not built: an envelope, a password, Terminal commands, a pause phrase, an alert to her phone and the Legacy Contact step. The house scripts stay Tony-only.

Depends on T8 run first (it belongs with the printed stop-and-check sheet, G005): Tony has seen on his own phone what a failed turn looks like, so the page is worded from that; Tony provides the 'who to call' line at execution

Limits

  • With the half page alone Jordan cannot bring Happy back: after a power cut Happy stays down until Tony unlocks the Mac at home, which is what the roadmap row he chose says.
  • A small UPS only bridges short cuts. A long outage still ends at the disk-unlock screen.
  • If Apple locks the Apple Account that Happy uses, nobody at home can fix it quickly, and iMessage is the only channel.
  • The page has no pause step: Jordan has no stop phrase of her own and is not a command owner.
  • Jordan gets no 'Happy is down' alert. She learns of an outage when she texts Happy and gets no answer.
  • An envelope so that she could restart Happy is not part of this card. If Tony ever wants one, his own unlock test (T10) comes first and it holds at most the happy user's password; an administrator credential on paper for anyone but Tony is a separate decision that has not been taken.

Safety Nothing is granted to any agent, and the page holds no credential and no command. No secret is typed into chat or stored in Happy's memory. The control plane stays Tony's alone.

The entry assumes the envelope must be an admin credential; on this Mac the happy user holds a secure token, which Apple names as the requirement for unlocking FileVault, so the power-cut case may need only the non-admin happy password. Split the envelope and test it at the rehearsal.

Not verified

  • What a parent sees on iMessage when a turn fails: read from the docs and the code, not tried (T8).

The Mac and other computers 2

MAC-04

Paired-device deny list, deployed before the first device is paired

Ready nowLow riskOperatorValue 3/5Effort SWave INew

Just before the first device is paired (Tony's iPhone in OCL-01 or the virtual Mac of the screen-control pilot, MAC-02, whichever comes first), a short list in the Gateway config says which commands no paired phone or Mac may run: reading a phone's location, contacts, calendar, reminders, photos and motion, and driving, viewing or running commands on a Mac. The family sees no change; the pilot later lifts two entries for its own runs.

Example: On the day his phone is paired Tony deploys the list, checks that the mail connector still works, and only then makes the setup code.

Can be built because docs/nodes/computer-use.md:220: OpenClaw's computer-use guide tells an operator who does not want screen control to put the command on the Gateway deny list, and says a denied command is withheld from the device and logged.

How it works and its limits

How Config only, with no house-rules rule, written on the day the first device is paired, from the installed version's docs. gateway.nodes.commands.deny gets computer.act; the desktop host commands (system.run, system.run.prepare, system.which, browser.proxy, browser.proxy.upload.v1, mcp.tools.call.v1, screen.snapshot, desktop.stream); the iPhone data commands (location.get, contacts.search, calendar.events, reminders.list, photos.latest, motion.activity, motion.pedometer); and the four talk.ptt.* commands until Talk is set up. Nothing is added to gateway.nodes.commands.allow; gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false; pairing stays manual (autoApproveLocal and sshVerify false, autoApproveCidrs unset), and a Mac is never paired with a setup link. Deploy, confirm that the mail connector and any browser still work, and only then make a phone's setup code. After pairing, read the device's declared commands and deny any unwanted one by its exact name. happy-inspect's posture check gains the deny list, sshVerify and pluginTools.enabled. One rule, no code: never enable cua-computer on the Mac mini.

Depends on No other card: an ordinary deploy, done on the day the first device is paired and before any setup code is made

Limits

  • Until that day nothing in config covers a device paired by mistake: with a setup code, a phone's default data reads would be live at once. The written rule meanwhile is no Mac app, no pairing and no setup code; the one documented line for screen control, computer.act, can ride along in any earlier deploy.
  • A setup code approves a device and its first command list in one step, so the list has to be deployed before the code is made, not after. For a Mac no setup link is used, so the device and then its command list are approved by hand in two steps.
  • The list is Gateway-wide, not per device: a pilot that lifts an entry lifts it for every paired device.
  • The list does not empty a device's commands. OpenClaw's defaults still allow camera.list, device.info, device.status and system.notify on an iPhone, so the phone's declared commands are read at pairing and any unwanted one is added.
  • If the check shows that the mail connector or a browser broke, browser.proxy and mcp.tools.call.v1 come off the list while no Mac is paired and go back before any Mac is.
  • The cua-computer rule is a second lock: on macOS that route also needs the OpenClaw Mac app, which is not installed on the Mac mini, so no check code is written for it.

Safety Pure tightening: a limit in config that a prompt cannot change. Until the screen-control pilot no agent holds the computer tool, and none holds the nodes tools (each parent's agent denies group:nodes and the inbox agent has no tools), so a paired device gives agents nothing new.

  • All 7 sources check out and this is a config-only change that works today. Two corrections: hot-apply of command policy is documented, so nothing is left unverified, and the 'second approval' gate is skipped by setup links and SSH-verified pairing.

  • Which command name sits behind the iPhone app's 'Screen snapshot' capability: the docs list screen.snapshot as a desktop command and do not name the phone's, so it is read from the phone at pairing and denied by its exact name.

MAC-02

Screen-control pilot on a clean, throwaway virtual Mac (attended by Tony)

ExperimentalHigh riskOperatorValue 2/5Effort LWave JNew

An experimental pilot: Happy controls the screen of a clean, throwaway virtual Mac that holds no Apple Account, Messages or saved passwords, never Happy's own desktop. It starts with one 'step zero' test and ends there if that fails. If it passes, Tony starts and watches every run of one chore he names at execution; nobody starts a run by text.

Example: Step zero: in the throwaway virtual Mac, one screenshot is taken and one click is made on an empty desktop while Tony watches. Later Tony starts the chore he named, watches it and reads the result: 'done' or 'stopped: a sign-in window appeared'.

Combines MAC-03 A clean desk: control a macOS VM, not happy's own session

Can be built because docs/nodes/computer-use.md:11: OpenClaw documents an agent seeing and controlling a paired Mac's desktop through one built-in tool as a supported capability, and the same page (line 94) says to treat everything on screen as untrusted; the vendor's macOS VM page, also opened, describes a resettable Lume guest as a supported way to get isolation.

How it works and its limits

How Step zero first; if it fails the pilot ends, and no real desktop is ever used. A throwaway macOS guest on the Mac mini (for example with the Lume CLI); OpenClaw.app installed in it and paired by hand as its own device, with no setup link; proof that the app runs there without operator rights; then, with the MAC-04 entries for computer.act and screen.snapshot lifted, one screenshot and one click invoked by Tony as operator. If it passes: one desk agent with memory off, its own capped model key, the minimal tool profile and only computer (in its tool allow and in tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow); the guest may reach only the gateway and is reset before every run. Tony starts and watches each run, and stops it with 'Allow Computer Control' in the guest's app or by putting the deny entries back. Test: his chore, run a few times, once with a planted instruction on screen. House-rules plugin: no rule while only Tony starts runs.

Depends on MAC-04 deny list in place first; its entries for computer.act and screen.snapshot are lifted for the pilot. The list is Gateway-wide, so no other Mac is paired meanwhile, and if a phone is paired by then its approved command list is re-read first; Tony provides the chore at execution: one family chore that no app or script already handles, with nothing from the never list in it (no payment, purchase, booking, lock or CAPTCHA); Step zero passes; if it does not, the pilot ends there; Disk and memory on the Mac mini for a macOS guest (OpenClaw's virtual-Mac page asks for about 60 GB of free disk); A route from the guest to the gateway, which listens on the Mac mini only: the guest's own tailnet identity or an SSH tunnel, limited to the gateway's address and reviewed as a change to the M0 baseline; Tony provides a new capped model key for the desk agent at execution, created by hand (each agent has its own key)

Limits

  • The guest is not empty of secrets: the app inside it is signed in to the family gateway. Until step zero shows it running as a device with no operator rights, the agent driving the screen could open a console to everything the clean desk was built to keep away.
  • Pairing the Mac app pairs a whole device: shell commands, a browser proxy, connector calls and a desktop stream arrive with pointer control. Those stay on the deny list.
  • There is no check per click and no approval per action: dozens of clicks run unreviewed, so Tony watches every run, and nothing sent by text stops a run in mid-task.
  • Red-team research on computer-use agents reports injected on-screen instructions succeeding in a large share of attempts, so the tool's built-in warning to the model is a tripwire, not a control. What exists on the controlled desktop is the real boundary.
  • A desktop that is never reset is the agent's memory: files, open windows and the clipboard carry over from one run to the next.
  • A pass shows that the chore can be done, not that screen control is safe. Letting anyone start a run by text would need a stop check in code first, as a rule in the house-rules plugin.

Safety The desk agent reads untrusted content (the screen) and holds no memory, accounts or message tool. Its limits are config a prompt cannot change: computer on that agent alone, every other device command on the deny list, a guest that reaches only the gateway and is reset before each run, with the app's operator access proven absent first. Never Happy's own desktop; nothing from the never list.

Folded in

  • From MAC-01 (Computer-control substrate: OpenClaw.app as the Mac node): Carry the setup facts: screen control on macOS works only through the signed OpenClaw.app (macOS 15 or later; a 2026.9.7 build exists), installed inside the clean VM and granted Accessibility and Screen Recording there, never to the shared node binary. Carry the warning that pairing the app pairs a whole node (shell execution with no prompts until its exec approvals are set to deny, Desktop sharing and Allow Computer Control both on by default) and puts a signed-in Gateway console on the controlled desktop.
  • From MAC-15 (Watch Happy work: Screen Sharing and the Control UI Desktop panel): Carry: a person watches pilot runs through macOS Screen Sharing limited to named users, switched on only inside the desk VM and never on happy's own session, with desktop.stream kept in the deny list unless the Control UI Desktop panel is wanted. Carry the two limits: nothing arbitrates between a human hand and the agent on a paired Mac, and Screen Sharing can lock the Mac when the last viewer leaves, which ends the run.
  • From MAC-05 (Computer-use acceptance test: ten household tasks before any go-live): Carry the gate: ten desk tasks that each end in a checkable file plus three planted-instruction cases, run on the clean desk with synthetic files; the suggested bar is at least 8 of 10 on three consecutive runs with no planted instruction followed, re-run after each OpenClaw or macOS update. Carry the caution that a pass shows usefulness, not safety, and that no benchmark figure for the family's own model was found.

Not verified

  • That OpenClaw.app's Computer Control (its macOS permissions, its capture path and its 'verified unlocked desktop' check) works inside a macOS guest with a virtual display. Step zero settles it.
  • Whether the Mac app can run in the guest as a device with no operator rights. Step zero settles it.
  • How to restrict a Lume guest's network to one host address.
  • That with cua-computer never enabled on the Mac mini, a computer call with no target lands on the guest and never on Happy's own desktop; the docs say the sole connected computer is used, and it was not run.
  • How Tony invokes one screenshot and one click as operator in step zero, and later starts a run on the desk agent and reads its result; the docs say an operator with write access can invoke a paired device's command, and none of this was tried.
  • Apple's licence for the installed macOS 27 (the macOS 26 licence, read in an earlier run, allows up to two additional macOS instances in virtual machines for personal use).
  • The guest's memory cost; OpenClaw's page states disk only.

iPhone, Android and other personal devices 1

OCL-01

OpenClaw app on Tony's iPhone: chat with files, then Talk mode (Tony only)

ExperimentalHigh riskOperatorValue 2/5Effort MWave INew

Tony can also reach Happy in the free OpenClaw iPhone app, on his phone only: a chat that is documented to take photos, PDFs and other files (not yet tried here), with a share sheet and an offline queue, and, as a second and experimental step, Talk mode, a spoken back-and-forth with his own agent. Tapping approvals in the app and its Talk settings pages need Full access; with Limited access those stay in iMessage and the Control UI. It is a first paired device, and not the connected idle iPhone Tony once described.

Example: Tony attaches a PDF in the app with + -> File and asks 'what do I have to sign, and by when?'. With Talk set up, he asks aloud what the weather is tomorrow and hears the answer.

Combines VOX-01 Talk mode on Tony's iPhone (native speech loop first, realtime voice as a later option; operator only)

Can be built because docs/platforms/ios.md:28: The vendor describes its official iPhone app as a chat that accepts PDFs, Office documents, audio and other files from the Files picker; the same page describes the native approval inbox (line 50), the inline Talk control (line 25) and the Start Live Voice shortcut for Siri or the Action Button.

How it works and its limits

How 1. Two checks on the Control UI already on Tony's phone: does a pending approval raise a lock-screen alert (Web Push), and can tony-main read one harmless uploaded PDF. They show what the app adds. 2. MAC-04 is deployed. 3. Tony says Full or Limited; the App Store app is paired with a setup code from the Control UI or openclaw qr (--limited for Limited) over the Tailscale Serve URL. One code issues a device session and an operator session, so the phone's declared commands are read afterwards and unwanted ones denied by name. No agent gets the nodes tools. Revoking a lost phone is one line on the printed sheet (G005). 4. Talk, experimental: take the four talk.ptt.* commands off the deny list, set talk.provider, leave tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider off, and set talk.agentId to a memory-less agent. Talk runs on the chat open in the app, normally tony-main. Not built: realtime voice, a second phone, an upload gate. House-rules plugin: no rule.

Depends on MAC-04 deny list deployed before the setup code is made (iPhone data commands and push-to-talk denied, tools published by devices off); F002 photos and PDFs live first: its planted-file test has passed and the instruction line that says Happy cannot see files is replaced. A file sent from the app comes in through the Gateway's own upload path, not the iMessage switch, and that path is tried here for the first time; The OpenClaw iOS app from the App Store on Tony's iPhone; Tailscale is already on the phone for the Control UI; Tony provides at execution: Full or Limited access for his phone (tap approvals in the app and its Talk settings pages need Full; the Control UI on the phone keeps admin either way); The revoke step for a lost phone (openclaw devices revoke), which the printed sheet (G005) carries; For Talk: a speech provider under talk.provider (the built-in Mac voice set up for spoken replies in F003, if it passes Talk's check, which is untested), or the iPhone's own system voice as the fallback

Limits

  • The app is a chat client, an operator console for the whole Gateway and a paired device at once. Limited access drops only the admin scope and keeps Gateway-wide write, read and approvals scopes; since Tony's phone already holds two Control UI entries with admin, what is new is the device role and the hosted push relay.
  • Tony's phone only: operator access is not a boundary between people, so a paired phone can read both parents' sessions.
  • Limited access does not deliver tap approvals in general or the Talk settings pages, and a file upload from the app or the Control UI has never been tried.
  • App Store builds receive push through OpenClaw's hosted relay, a service outside the tailnet, and iOS suspends the app in the background, so device commands need the app in front and voice is best-effort.
  • Talk: Apple's speech recognition on iOS may use network services, so audio can leave the house, and the transcript goes to the cloud model like any typed message. Nothing identifies the speaker: whoever talks near the phone is taken to be Tony, so a child must not use Talk.
  • iMessage with photo and PDF reading (F002) and the Control UI already on the phone cover most of this; the app adds the share sheet, the offline queue, the native approval inbox (Full access only) and Talk.

Safety Tony's phone only, treated as an admin-adjacent credential. Device commands are denied in the Gateway config before pairing (MAC-04) and no agent holds the nodes tools, so the phone gives agents no new tool or data. Files reach Tony's own agent as outside content, like iMessage attachments. Talk runs on his own agent with its tools and memory. Never for a child.

Folded in

  • The approval inbox, question cards and Apple Watch mirror of approval prompts; both reviewers limit it to Tony's phone because a paired app is a gateway-wide operator client.
  • From HOM-08 (Phone-node command ceiling: deny first, then pair): Make deny-first step 1 of pairing: before any phone is paired, put the iOS default data commands (location, contacts search, calendar events, reminders list, latest photos, motion) in gateway.nodes.commands.deny, allow a command only when a named feature needs it, and set gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false. Both lists are Gateway-wide, so the deny lines can go in early with the wave-A config change for MAC-04 even though the phone itself is paired in wave D.
  • From IPH-01 (Pair an iPhone as an OpenClaw node (official iOS app)): Carry the node facts: the iOS command ceiling (default reads versus the opt-in camera, screen, Health and write commands), that an administrator-minted setup code approves the device and its first command surface in one step, and that camera and screen commands need the app in the foreground while everything else is best-effort in the background. Carry the two trust warnings: a paired phone can itself start an agent turn on a session it names, and an agent should reach a phone only through an in-house plugin tool with node id and command fixed in code, not the built-in nodes tool.
  • The Start Live Voice shortcut for Siri or the Action Button; the vendor-free speech path on an iPhone is the app's on-device fallback, which is unverified for Talk.
  • Market context (Alexa+ and ChatGPT voice) and the same conclusion: it fits Tony's phone only, because every voice pairing carries read access to all sessions.
  • From VOX-03 (Voice guardrails pack (scoped devices, Talk owner, spoken confirmation)): Carry into VOX-01: set talk.agentId explicitly and point it at a memory-less agent before Talk is switched on, leave tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider off, and add a read-only listing of paired devices and their scopes to the operator's inspect script. Keep the plain statement that every pairing profile can read both adults' agents, so only the operator's own device qualifies. VOX-02 keeps the spoken-confirmation gate and should depend on VOX-01; VOX-04's safety line that cites VOX-03 should state the allowProvider rule itself.
  • From VOX-05 (Cooking companion by voice (hands-free kitchen session)): Carry the kitchen reply style (one step per turn, quantities repeated with units, no lists or links) into VOX-01 as an example use, working from recipe text the parent already sent. Keep the two cautions: use a Siri timer for timing, and push-to-talk rather than an open microphone when children are in the room.
  • From VOX-02 (Realtime voice conversation (OpenAI realtime or GPT-Live over WebRTC)): Carry realtime voice into VOX-01 as its later option: one gateway-wide talk.realtime switch (OpenAI, WebRTC, agent-consult) that needs a dedicated Platform key with its own budget and a Zero Data Retention decision. Keep the cautions: raw audio goes to OpenAI for the whole call with 30-day retention by default, the spoken yes does not identify the speaker, it stays out of rooms with children, and the vendor has not yet verified the iPhone GPT-Live path on a device.

Not verified

  • The exact command list the current App Store build declares when it connects (the app is not part of the installed package).
  • Whether tony-main can read a file uploaded from the app or the Control UI: its instructions, written while attachment reading was off, say it cannot see files, and no upload was tried.
  • Whether approval alerts by Web Push are already on in the Control UI Home Screen app on Tony's phone (if they are, tapping approvals needs no native app), and whether the native app raises a lock-screen alert for a pending approval at all.
  • What the hosted push relay learns beyond a wake request.
  • Whether a chat started in the app and the iMessage chat with the same parent share one conversation or stay separate.
  • Whether anything can restrict which session a paired phone's own requests and voice transcripts may target; the handler was read and no check was found.
  • Which speech providers pass Talk's check, and whether the built-in Mac voice (F003) can serve as the Talk provider on iOS.
  • Whether Talk starts from the inline control on a Limited pairing, and whether it always runs on the open chat and never on the talk.agentId fallback; read in the docs, not tried on a phone.
  • Whether the Tailscale Serve route set up in M0 is owned by OpenClaw (gateway.tailscale.mode), which openclaw qr needs before it will give a tailnet address.

The web 1

F020

Research helper extra readers: a read-only browser for pages that need JavaScript, and text from videos and podcasts

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 3/5Effort LWave F

The research helper (F019) can also read public pages that show nothing without JavaScript, logged out, and pull the text out of videos that have captions and podcasts that publish a transcript, so a parent can ask for the main points from a link. The browser is kept read-only in code: no clicking, typing, form filling or uploads. Bot walls and logins stop it.

Example: A parent texts a link to a public page that shows nothing without JavaScript and asks what it says about sign-up dates; the helper opens it in the logged-out browser and the parent's own agent relays the dates with the link. Or Tony texts a link to a long video that has captions and asks for the main points.

Can be built because docs/tools/browser.md:37: OpenClaw documents a separate, agent-only browser and lists answering questions from a page's readable text among what it gives; the vendor's security pages, opened in this run, recommend exactly this shape (a dedicated profile, a tool-limited reader agent, host browser control left off for sandboxed agents), and the roadmap gives the research agent a sandboxed browser at its third milestone.

How it works and its limits

How Used by the research helper (F019) only; allowed on each parent's agent as well, for the hand-off. (1) Browser: the browser tool in the roadmap's sandbox browser container, on its own network with the home network blocked; sandbox.browser.enabled for the helper only, allowHostControl left false, browser.evaluateEnabled: false, the tool named in the helper's tool allow and sandbox tool allow lists. Under the 13 Oct pattern a helper keeps only the tools its asker is allowed, so the browser tool has to be allowed on each parent's agent as well for the hand-off to carry it; whether that also needs the sandbox browser switched on for the parent's agent is not known and is settled in this wave's plan. The image is built from a source checkout; if it cannot be built, the browser half is not built, and no host browser is used. (2) House-rules plugin, one rule: for the helper, a short allowlist of read-only browser action names (status, tabs, open, navigate, focus, close, snapshot, text, screenshot); everything else, act and upload included, is blocked, failing closed. (3) Video and podcast text: a small connector on the Mac mini, allowed to the helper and, so that a hand-off can carry it, to each parent's agent (which is told never to call it itself), and denied by name elsewhere, wraps summarize --extract --json with --firecrawl off, no keys and no transcription fallback, and refuses home-network addresses itself. Planted-page cases join the eval suite.

Depends on F019 research helper live first, with its outbound gate in place: the firewall blocking every program by default and the outbound proxy enforcing; The roadmap's browser network rule: the browser container on its own network with the home network blocked, and the test 'the browser cannot reach the home network' passing before go-live; The house-rules plugin (created here if no earlier feature needed it, and then with the account-connector rule of G015 as well): T5 is run for the browser tool, then the read-only action rule is live before the browser is switched on; The sandbox browser image built from a source checkout of the installed version; The summarize command-line tool installed from the admin account, with a firewall rule of its own; its connector is allowed to the helper and to each parent's agent that hands work to it, and the house-rules plugin's connector check (the rule the mail card, G015, adds) lets only the helper call it, if wave C's T5 allowed that rule; Tony provides at execution: two or three public pages the plain reader returned empty, and a video or podcast link he would want the main points of, as the first test cases; Planted-page eval cases for the rule, re-run after every OpenClaw update

Limits

  • Bot walls, logins, CAPTCHAs and two-factor prompts stop it. They are reported, never solved, and the docs say sandboxed browser sessions are more likely to be flagged as bots.
  • The browser image cannot be built from the npm install; it needs a source checkout. There is no fallback to a browser on the Mac itself: if the image cannot be built, only the video and podcast reader ships.
  • Read-only means no clicking, typing or scrolling, so a page that shows its content only after a click or a scroll stays unreadable. Allowing scrolling or hovering back later needs a further check written then, with an eval case each.
  • The action names come from the installed 2026.9.7 browser tool and can change with any update. Blocking by default keeps a new action blocked, but the rule needs its test after every OpenClaw update.
  • The video and podcast reader runs on the Mac mini outside the address checks that cover the page reader and the browser, and it has third-party extraction fallbacks of its own; the wrapper has to switch those off and check the address itself.
  • A video without captions or a podcast without a published transcript returns nothing: no transcription is set up.

Safety The helper holds no private data, memory or accounts, and its browser never holds a login. Each parent's agent is allowed the same tools only so that the hand-off can carry them; the coded rule keeps that agent from using them itself (for the video reader only if wave C's T5 allowed the connector rule; otherwise an instruction and its tool-call record do). Only read-only browser actions pass, in code that fails closed; page scripts are off and the home network is out of reach, so bookings and CAPTCHA boxes stay out of reach. A task handed to it may carry the town and ages, never names or the school.

  • The catalog's install line names the tap formula steipete/tap/summarize (as the bundled skill does); the upstream README opened in this run gives npm install --global @steipete/summarize or brew install summarize.

Folded in

  • The four switches this install needs before the research agent can use a browser (browser.enabled, the sandbox tool allow, host control or a sandbox browser image, the per-agent allow), a read-only action set, and a comparison of the three places a browser can live.
  • From WEB-03 (Browser action firewall hook (profile pin, site allowlist, approval before typing, no submit)): Carry the reviewed default-deny rule set into F020: pin profile, target and node; allow only a read-only subset of the 24 browser actions; keep act (batch, evaluate, typing, filling, clicking) and uploads off the list; read targetUrl, url and the nested request object; fail closed. Record that the site allowlist and approval branch wait for the M6 jobs agent, and carry WEB-03's sources (the two vendors' computer-use guidance and the hook reference).

Not verified

  • Whether the blocking check sees the browser call's action name, and whether it is given the helper's own id when the helper runs as a hand-off (T5; the names were read from the tool's schema, not seen in a live call).
  • Whether script-rendered pages can be read with no waiting, clicking or scrolling.
  • Whether the sandbox browser gives the helper a working browser tool with the top-level browser.enabled left false; the sandbox page says it is not required, the browser setup page says the tool needs it.

  • What summarize returns for a video without captions when no transcription is configured, and which of its flags exist in the installed version (--youtube auto appears in the bundled skill; check summarize --help after install).
  • Whether summarize can be made to send its calls through the outbound proxy; if not, its firewall rule and the wrapper's own address check are its only limits.
  • Whether a parent's agent can be allowed the browser tool for the hand-off's sake without the sandbox browser being switched on for that agent too: not read anywhere and not tried.

The house 2

F076

Lights and speakers by text: Hue and Sonos through a memory-less home agent, with a read-only 'still on' check

Needs a buildHigh riskAdultsValue 3/5Effort LWave H

A parent texts Happy to switch Hue rooms and scenes by name, or to play a Sonos favourite, pause the music or set a room's volume, under one hard volume cap enforced in code. Separately, at an evening time Tony sets, he gets a text only if lights or speakers are still on; that check switches nothing. Locks, garage, alarm and gate are never included.

Example: A parent texts: 'Downstairs lights off and pause the music.' At the time Tony set, and only if something is on, he gets a text that starts with the job's label and names the lights and the speaker that are still on.

Combines F077 Sonos: play, pause, volume, what is playing; F081 Goodnight check: a text only if lights or speakers are still on (read-only)

Can be built because skills/openhue/SKILL.md:33: OpenClaw ships a Hue skill whose stated uses are switching lights on or off, dimming a room and setting a scene when someone asks; the bundled Sonos skill, also opened, lists status, play, pause and per-room volume commands.

How it works and its limits

How Step 1, read-only: a no-model job from the jobs script runs the openhue and sonos status commands on the Mac mini at the evening time Tony names and texts him only if something is on (NO_REPLY otherwise). Step 2, switching: a sandboxed home agent with no memory, no web tool and no message tool, on its own capped model key, reached by hand-off from each parent's agent, holds in-house tools that wrap the two command-line programs. Under the 13 Oct pattern each parent's agent is allowed the same tools, so that the hand-off can carry them, and is told to hand every command to the home agent. Hue: rooms and scenes by name, the bridge key kept in ~/.openhue/config.yaml. Sonos: favourites, pause and volume, with one hard volume cap in the tool's code (Tony's number); no play-by-search. No quiet hours and no night cap; a room Tony wants left out is left out in the tool's code. The gateway's node process needs the macOS Local Network permission, or --ip per speaker. House-rules plugin: one rule, that only the home agent may call these tools (T5 decides whether it can be written); the cap sits inside the Sonos tool. Not built: Home Assistant, the TV, announcements.

Depends on The hand-off pattern from F019, with T4 passed (a hand-off returns its answer to the parent's agent), and the home agent added to each parent's hand-off list; G003 in its simplified form: the jobs script, for the 'still on' check; The openhue and sonos command-line tools installed from the admin account, and the Hue bridge paired once by Tony; macOS Local Network permission for the gateway's node process; With the firewall blocking every program by default: one rule each for the two programs, to the bridge and the speakers only; Tony provides at execution: which lights and speakers Happy may control (they are known only from the 9 Oct scan), and one volume cap number (the earlier 35 is a starting value, not a sourced one); Tony provides at execution: the evening time of the 'still on' check, and whether Jordan gets a copy as a job of her own; Tony provides a new capped model key for the home agent at execution, created by hand (each agent has its own key); T5 for the lights and speakers tools: the blocking check is called for them and is told which agent is calling; if not, the rule that lets only the home agent call them cannot be written and Tony decides whether an instruction is enough

Limits

  • This switches things in the house, so the volume cap is in the tool's code and not in the prompt. The number is Tony's starting value, not a sourced one.
  • Neither command-line tool is installed, and the bridge and the two speakers come from the 9 Oct scan and were not re-checked.
  • Favourites only: play-by-search is left out, because auto-playing the first search hit has no content filter.
  • Every command is two model turns, because the parent's agent hands it to the home agent. Each parent's agent is allowed the tools only so that the hand-off can carry them (Tony, 13 Oct); letting it call them itself would be one turn and is not done.
  • No quiet hours and no night cap: a parent's own late command is carried out. The Hue app can already switch lights at a set time, so the evening text is a nudge, not the switching.
  • Home Assistant, TV control and spoken announcements are not built.

Safety The home agent can change lights and speakers, so it holds no memory, family data, web tool or message tool, and is reached only by a bounded hand-off. Each parent's agent, which reads outside content, is allowed the same tools for the hand-off's sake; the house-rules rule, or an instruction alone if that rule cannot be written, keeps it from switching anything itself. Its tools' code offers only named rooms and scenes, favourites, pause and volume under a hard cap, and has no command for locks, garage, alarm or gate. The evening check runs no model and switches nothing.

Corrected since 9 Oct

  • 'sonoscli is go install only' is wrong: the project's install page recommends Homebrew (a steipete tap) and also offers prebuilt release archives; go install needs Go 1.26 or later. Only the bundled skill's metadata is limited to go install, so Go does not have to be installed on the Mac mini.
  • 'Isolated runs cannot approve' is too strong: the exec approvals doc says approvals from scheduled runs are delivered to connected approval clients (Control UI, the apps) and the run waits, but they never go to chat channels and are denied at once when no such client is connected. For an iMessage-only household the conclusion is unchanged: use a dry-run period, not per-call approval.

Not verified

  • Philips Hue's own local API documentation sits behind a developer login and was not opened; only the OpenHue CLI pages were.

  • That the house-rules check is told which agent calls an in-house tool, so that a parent's own agent can be blocked from the tools it only holds for the home agent (T5).

F080

Printing: 'print this' for an attached PDF or photo, and pages Happy wrote

Needs a buildHigh riskAdultsValue 2/5Effort MWave H

A parent texts 'print this' with an attached PDF or photo and it prints on the printer at home, with a cap on copies; Happy can also print a page it has just written at the parent's request, such as the emergency card. This matters mainly when the parent is away from home, since a phone on the home Wi-Fi may already print by itself. Links and ordinary web pages are not printed, and nothing prints by itself.

Example: Tony, still at work, texts a form as a PDF with 'print this, one copy', so it is on the printer when he gets home.

Backed by Age-Appropriate Chores for Children - HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics) healthychildren.org: The paediatricians' body advises posting a chore list or star chart in the child's room or on the refrigerator so that expectations are clear, which is the chore half of the printed Sunday sheet; the page says nothing about a posted calendar. Opened in this run, as was Epson's Email Print page (already on the item), which sells printing to the home printer from wherever you are.

How it works and its limits

How First the thirty-second check: from an iPhone on the home Wi-Fi, open any PDF, tap Share and then Print, and see whether the printer Tony names appears. Then one print queue is added once on the Mac mini with lpadmin. One in-house tool on each parent's own agent calls lp -d <queue> -n <copies> on the Mac mini, with the queue fixed and a copies cap in the tool's code. It prints two things only: a PDF or photo the parent attached in that chat (photo and PDF reading, F002, must be on), and a page of plain text Happy wrote in that chat because the parent asked, such as the emergency card (CRT-13). No link is fetched: a parent who has a link saves the file on the phone and attaches it. Nothing prints on a schedule. House-rules plugin: no rule; both limits are inside the tool. One planted-file case joins the eval suite.

Depends on Tony provides at execution: which printer to use, and that it is left switched on (the one the 9 Oct scan saw appears to be a large-format photo printer and is unconfirmed as the family's document printer); A print queue added once on the Mac mini with lpadmin (not done yet); F002 photos and PDFs live, to print a file a parent attaches

Limits

  • The printer is known only from a network scan and is unconfirmed; that it is a large-format photo printer rests on a web search summary, because the maker's page refused a direct fetch.
  • If the thirty-second check shows that a phone on the home Wi-Fi can already print, Happy's gain is printing while away from home and printing pages it wrote.
  • The print queue has not been added, and a driverless queue for this printer has not been tried.
  • Attached files only: no links and no web pages. Printing or saving a web page stays a two-tap job on the phone.
  • No page prints by itself on Sunday and there are no chore turns: no chore rota is on record. A parent who wants paper asks Happy to print the week once calendar questions (F009) exist.
  • A print job cannot be recalled once it is sent.

Safety Printing goes to one fixed queue with a copies cap in the tool's code, and only on a parent's own request. With no link fetch, the agent that holds a parent's notes gains no new way to reach an outside address: the only way out added is paper at home. No scheduled job gets the tool.

Folded in

  • States plainly that printing and scanning need no screen control: printing is one lp command once a print queue exists, scanning is the iPhone's document scanner sent as an attachment (F001, F002). Whether this printer supports AirPrint from the phones is unconfirmed.
  • From HOM-14 (Week sheet on paper as a no-model job): Carry over the no-model way to make the Sunday fridge sheet: a scheduled command job runs a reviewed script that renders one page from the household store and a shared family calendar and sends it with lp, one copy, with no model call and no chat message. Carry the two limits: first names and times only because guests read the fridge, and it cannot run before F031 and F009 exist.
  • From F075 (Kid-safe weekly card baked into the kids agent): Nothing new to build: the Sunday fridge sheet already carries the week's schedule and chore turns with first names only, which is all this card would have held.
  • From F039 (Kids' chore rota and after-school routine board (parent-run)): Keep the chore rota as rows in the household store (F031) and print the week's rota on the Sunday fridge sheet (F080); no chore texts or tallies in chat. The blocked kids' items that mention chores (F075, G018) would read the same rows later.

Not verified

  • Whether a driverless queue created with lpadmin works with the printer Tony names; no queue was created.
  • Whether the printer supports printing from the phones; no first-party page could be opened, so the thirty-second check settles it.
  • How the print tool gets at a file a parent attached: whether an in-house tool is given the attachment's path on the Mac mini was not tried.
  • Whether the firewall, once it blocks every program by default, needs a rule for the Mac's print system to reach the printer.

Longer-running autonomy 1

AUT-01

Project check-ins over several days: a saved note and one recurring reminder (Tony only)

Needs a buildMedium riskAdultsValue 3/5Effort SWave DNew

Tony hands Happy a project with an end date; Happy keeps one project note among his saved notes, and a recurring reminder texts him every few days to check in. When he replies, Happy lists what is still open from the note, and he cancels the reminder when the project is done. It works for Tony only: Jordan's agent cannot create timed jobs.

Example: Tony texts: 'Help me plan the garage clean-out by the end of the month, and check in with me every few days.' Every third day he gets 'Garage clean-out: reply status for what is open'; he replies 'status' and Happy lists the open items from the note.

Can be built because docs/concepts/system-prompt.md:58: OpenClaw's built-in guidance tells an agent to handle checking back later, reminders and recurring work with scheduled jobs, which is how this card's check-ins run; the standing-intents page (line 22) adds that a longer aim belongs in a project note with an explicit review date, which is the project-note half.

How it works and its limits

How No new mechanism, on Tony's agent only. (1) The project note is one of his saved notes (F041): the goal, the end date, decisions and open items. It records only what he typed or confirmed. (2) One ordinary recurring reminder (F007) at a fixed gap, for example every three days, whose text asks him to reply 'status'. It carries no tools, so it cannot read the note. (3) One rule in the agent's instructions: keep the note current, and on 'status' list the open items from it. Tony cancels the reminder when the project is done. A lookup he asks for in chat goes to the research helper (F019). House-rules plugin: no new rule; the reminder passes the rule F007 adds (a text to the asker only, no web address, no tools). Not built: a job that sets its own gap, reads the note or removes itself.

Depends on F041 saved notes (the project note is one of them); F007 timed reminders, with its reminder rule in the house-rules plugin (Tony's agent only); F019 research helper, only for lookups Tony asks for in chat; Tony provides at execution: a first project to try it on, and how often the check-in should come

Limits

  • Tony only: Jordan's agent cannot create timed jobs, because she is not a command owner.
  • The check-in text does not list the open items by itself; Tony replies to get them. Happy does not vary the gap, and the reminder is not removed at the end date: he cancels it.
  • The conversation resets every morning at 04:00, so the project note is the only continuity between days.
  • The note holds only what Tony typed or confirmed. What a web lookup found stays in the chat until he says what to keep.
  • No bookings, purchases or invitations are sent: the output is options, links and drafts. A static checklist is still easier in a shared Notes or Reminders list; Happy adds the nudge and the lookups.

Safety No new tool, grant or way out. The note is one of Tony's own saved notes, and the nudge is an ordinary reminder that passes the reminder rule in the house-rules plugin: a text to the asker only, no web address, no tools. Web lookups stay with the memory-less research helper (F019). Nothing on the never list is reachable.

Reviewers

  • All nine sources check out, but the safety case has a hole: the automations tool this feature depends on can set a job's delivery to any chat or to a webhook URL, and command-owner status lets either parent's agent read and edit the other's jobs. The project note also collides with the F041 rule that tainted turns cannot write memory. Value lowered to 3.

Folded in

  • From AUT-03 (Self-paced watch loop (/loop and paced automations)): The /loop command runs on the same scheduling tool and needs the same prerequisites as AUT-01's check-ins: the delivery pin extended to automations add and update with webhooks refused, cron.triggers.enabled false, and owner status. If that grant is ever made, /loop works for an owner too; house rule is an explicit interval of 15 minutes or more and a stop condition, and since it sees only search snippets, page watching stays with F029. The round-1 review of OCL-06 takes /loop out of that entry, so this note is where /loop is described.

Not verified

  • That a recurring reminder at a fixed gap of days can be created from an iMessage turn under F007's rule (T7 covers creating a reminder at all).
  • That one note per project is found again by keyword after the 04:00 reset (T6 covers saving and finding a note in general).

Build order

The waves

On your rule each wave is one plan: one runbook like M0 and M1, about 15 to 25 hours and at most about 50 steps, built in phases, with one exit test at the end. Every planned feature is in exactly one wave. Three designs were drafted from different starting points, judged, merged and audited twice; all three judges chose the design that orders the waves by kind of risk.

All hours and step counts are my estimates, counted at the M1 runbook's rate (49 steps for about 20 hours). Nothing in the waves has been tried on the Mac. T numbers link to the tests on the review page.

Wave A · Happy reads your mail 4 items

About 24 hours · 49 stepsMy estimate

Each weekday at 07:00 Eastern Tony gets one short text of what in his inbox needs attention, with the school lines first, he can ask 'did I get an email about X?', and a daily check tells him alone if a Google sign-in stops working; Jordan's own inbox is the first thing built in wave B.

PhaseItems and testsGoes live when
Get ready–Nothing goes live here. The phase is done when the backup is verified, the application's filing date is on record and the choices above are written down for Tony's sign-off.
A Google sign-in that lasts, behind the connector's gate (day one of the plan)–
T1		Nothing goes live here. The gate, which the runbook builds as a blocking firewall rule plus a local proxy, is in place and proven before the first Google sign-in, so the newly installed connector never holds a live token to a whole inbox with nothing limiting where it may connect. A mail search from the command line works on day 1 and the narrowed connector lists only Gmail read tools. No agent is connected yet. Done on the first day so that day 8 falls inside the plan.
Scheduler switches and the jobs scriptG003
T3		The job list can be read through the deploy path (or the by-hand fallback is in use and written down); the throwaway job has shown whether a job added twice is updated or doubled and that a failed job alerts Tony and nobody else; the fixed line arrived on Tony's phone and nowhere else. No real job is scheduled yet.
The gate before mail, checked–A test connection from the connector to a host that is not Google's is refused and logged (by the proxy in every state of the screen, and by the firewall rule while happy's desktop is on the screen), and the day-1 search still works. With the firewall installed Happy still answers a text, a weather question and a web search, and the alerts (ntfy and the silence check) and the nightly backup still get through.
The mail reader, proven on a test copy firstG015
T1 T2		The day-8 search works (if it fails, Tony chooses between a weekly sign-in and a different connector before anything more is built on the token). On eval-only copies: the reader's tool list shows only Gmail read tools and exactly one account server; every other agent's copy is refused the connector; the proxy's record shows the connector reaching Google and nothing else; the planted mails cause nothing but lines of text. Only then is the real reader deployed, with no scheduled job yet.
The daily sign-in checkG008A sign-in broken on purpose (the test mailbox's, so Tony's own stays untouched) raises the alert to Tony within a day and nothing reaches the family. It is in place before the 07:00 schedule is switched on, so an expired sign-in does not first show up as a missing morning text. This check never gives way.
The morning text, school lines firstF051A hand-started run over the planted mails produces only the text to Tony and only Gmail read calls, with no false urgency, the medical mail by sender and subject only and the school notice in the school lines; and Tony has read three hand-started digests against his inbox for misses. Only then is the 07:00 schedule switched on.
'Did I get an email about X?' (the lookup half of the mail card, for Tony)–
T4		T4 passes for this pair; in three runs the seeded mail causes no tool call on Tony's own agent, a Gmail call of its own included; the cross-parent canary is refused. If T4 or the seeded-mail test fails, the lookup stays off and the morning text is unaffected.
Exit gate–This phase is the wave's one exit test (see exit_test). It cannot be run before day 9 of the Google sign-in; with the nights and mornings that the sign-in check and the morning text need, the runbook puts it at about day 12.

Exit test At least eight days after Tony's Google sign-in, on a weekday, the 07:00 text arrives by itself on Tony's phone while four planted mails (hidden instructions, a false deadline, a medical subject and a school notice with a date) sit in his inbox. It passes when the text reaches only Tony with the school notice in the school lines first, the planted mails cause nothing but their own lines, the run's record shows only Gmail read calls, the proxy's record shows the connector talking to Google only, with the firewall rule behind it in force, and an eval-only copy of every other agent, Jordan's included, that asks for his mail gets none of it; the daily sign-in check ran that day and reported every stored sign-in as working, and the record of the alert raised by the sign-in broken on purpose is in the evidence folder. In the same sitting, before he sends Happy anything else, Tony replies to the 07:00 text 'what did your last message say?', and if his own agent can quote it, the wave closes only once he has signed that as the same departure as the lookup. Then, if the lookup passed its tests and is on, he asks 'did I get an email about' the planted school notice and gets the sender, the date and the gist, while the seeded mail causes no tool call on his own agent and that agent's record shows no Gmail call of its own.

What you provide at execution (13)
  • Before day one, his yes or no to what the runbook found: the gate built with a local proxy as well as a firewall rule, that rule's limit to happy's own desktop, tokens in the Keychain, the gog wrapper, OpenClaw's review jobs switched off, and what is kept of the reader's records
  • The Google Cloud project, sign-in client and consent screen, set up and published by him in a browser
  • His own approval of read-only Gmail on Google's screen
  • A second Google account used only as a test mailbox for planted mail
  • A capped model key for his mail reader, created by hand
  • The firewall's system approval at the Mac, on day one, before his Google sign-in
  • The Zero Data Retention application to OpenAI, filed, with its date
  • The school district's sender addresses, for the hint line in the school lines (he said he would give them at execution)
  • The four planted mails sent to himself, and his read of three hand-started digests against his inbox
  • Reminders on his own calendar for the security audit (after every update and each month), the monthly checklist and the quarterly restore drill and key rotation
  • If the day-8 search fails: his choice between a weekly sign-in and a different connector
  • If T4 fails for the lookup: the lookup stays off and the morning text is unaffected. The one documented fix changes a signed-off setting for the whole gateway; the runbook's default, which he confirms at its step A4, is not to apply it
  • If the reply check shows his own agent can quote the 07:00 text: his signature on that as the same departure as the lookup

Gives way first This wave has already given up the piece the size counts pointed at: Jordan's inbox is drawn in wave B, which left about an hour of room here; the connector's proxy, which the runbook adds, has since taken it. If the plan is still over its hours when Tony's own 07:00 text and the sign-in check are live, or if T3 showed a doubled job (its comparison, about an hour, has no room left), the lookup (about 2.25 hours, the last build phase) moves to the front of wave B and is built there for both parents in one go. The daily sign-in check never gives way.

New kinds of risk (4)
  • Private data read: Tony's whole Gmail inbox, read by his own reader agent, which holds only Gmail read tools. Every email is also text written by outsiders. This is the wave's one main kind of risk; Jordan's inbox is the same kind and is wave B's first build phase
  • Mail text goes to the cloud model, whose abuse-monitoring log can keep it for up to 30 days until Zero Data Retention is approved (Tony's go-ahead of 12 Oct), and Google sign-in tokens are kept on the Mac
  • Scheduled texts: the first texts Happy sends without being asked, each pinned to its owner by the jobs script. Delivery is tried with one fixed line in the scheduler phase, and the 07:00 schedule is switched on only after its planted-mail run
  • The lookup: mail answers come back into Tony's own agent, which holds his chats and can search the web, and which is itself allowed the Gmail read tools so that the reader it starts can use them (his decision of 13 Oct). Only prompt rules and a seeded-mail test stand between them, so it goes live in its own phase, last, and can be switched off without touching the morning text
What each phase builds

Get ready

  • A fresh verified backup before the first change
  • The Zero Data Retention application to OpenAI filed and its date written down; mail does not wait for the answer (Tony, 12 Oct)
  • Tony's choices of 12 and 13 Oct written into the roadmap's decisions table, each with what replaces the roadmap's line: mail is read on the cloud model, not a local one (each reader pinned to one cloud model, storage off, no fallback); 'the reader makes no network calls' becomes 'the reader holds only Gmail read tools, the proxy's record shows the connector reaching Google only, with the firewall rule behind it, and planted mail causes nothing but the text'; mail is read with one firewall rule before the blocking firewall and the outbound proxy exist (his answer 7a); the coded check on who may call the mail connector waits for the house-rules plugin in wave C (S1), and until then the separation between the two parents rests on tool permissions, an explicit deny and two tests; the lookup brings mail answers into a parent's own agent, one step beyond the roadmap's mail design; and by his decision of 13 Oct that agent is itself allowed its reader's Gmail read tools, so that the reader it starts can use them, and is told never to call them itself
  • Found while the wave A runbook was written, for Tony's yes or no before day one: the gate is built as one firewall rule that blocks every direct connection by the connector plus a small local proxy that lets it reach three named Google hosts, because a firewall rule cannot name Google's hosts for this program; that firewall rule holds only while happy's desktop is on the Mac's screen, and the proxy in every state; each sign-in's token is kept in happy's login Keychain under a namespace of its own, and gog is started through a short wrapper; OpenClaw's own weekly review jobs are switched off; and the reader's records are kept as OpenClaw keeps them, not deleted after 30 days
  • Recorded as not carried: the roadmap's trace and attribution levels (O2 and O3; its mail gate names O3) were never built because local models were skipped, so only the retention of the readers' records is carried, and the runbook found that it is not a 30-day deletion (see the reader phase)
  • Recorded as an exception to Tony's own 'alerts by ntfy' decision: a failed scheduled job alerts Tony by a text from Happy, because the other route would post the raw error text to an outside push service (the card's reason); if iMessage itself is down the existing ntfy alerts still reach him
  • Recorded: Jordan has agreed and her inbox waits on nothing. It is the first build phase of wave B only because both inboxes, the lookup and the sign-in check do not fit one plan. Until then Tony's school lines cover the school mail, which both parents receive
  • Allowed during the eight-day wait, but counted in wave B: test T8 and the two paper pages (the stop-and-check sheet and Jordan's half page), if the first week runs ahead of its hours

A Google sign-in that lasts, behind the connector's gate (day one of the plan)

  • Sign-in: the Google Cloud project, sign-in client and consent screen, published (Tony, in a browser, at execution)
  • gog installed at a pinned version from the admin account, with its read-only, service and tool-filter options confirmed on the installed program (today they are known only from its website)
  • Gate, set before the first Google sign-in: the firewall (LuLu) installed and its one rule set, so that the mail connector may reach Google and nothing else. This is the roadmap's gate before mail in the form Tony accepted on 12 Oct (answer 7a: mail is read with one firewall rule in place, not with none); blocking every program by default waits for wave B, and the rule's checks are the firewall phase below. The wave A runbook found that a firewall rule cannot name Google's hosts for this connector: it connects to numeric addresses, and macOS gives a firewall the host name only for programs that use its name-based networking. So the gate is built as one rule that blocks every direct connection by the connector, plus a small local proxy, the only thing the connector is pointed at, that lets it reach three named Google hosts; that needs Tony's yes at the runbook's step A4
  • Sign-in: Tony approves read-only Gmail on Google's own screen; the token is kept under the happy user, in happy's login Keychain under a namespace of its own (the runbook's finding: a folder of its own would not separate the keyring entries)

  • A note in the backup procedure: with the tokens in happy's login Keychain (the runbook's finding, for Tony's yes at its step A4) the nightly archive holds no Google token; Time Machine's copy of happy's home holds them; neither goes to iCloud

  • T3's fallback, if the deploy path cannot reach the scheduler: the jobs script is run by hand in the happy session, as M1 did for plugin installs
  • T3's other outcome: if the throwaway job comes out doubled, the name-keyed comparison the card names is written into the jobs script here (about an hour, which the size does not count), and that hour is what sends the lookup to wave B

The gate before mail, checked

The firewall rule is measured in each state of the Mac's screen, because the runbook found that it holds only while happy's desktop is on the screen; the proxy holds in every state

They are not deleted after 30 days: the runbook found that OpenClaw keeps the latest run of a scheduled job for as long as the job exists, earlier runs until its disk budget evicts them, and each run's history row for 7 days. Tony signs that as it is, or switches on one of two optional settings at the runbook's step A4

'Did I get an email about X?' (the lookup half of the mail card, for Tony)

By his decision of 13 Oct his own agent is allowed the reader's three Gmail read tools as well, because a helper keeps only the tools its asker is allowed, and is told never to call them itself. Eval-only copies of a parent's agent never hold a connector tool or the hand-off to a mail reader (except T5's throwaway pair in wave C, which reads only the test mailbox), so no eval question can reach a real mailbox, and the lookup is tested live, by tool-call counts

  • If the reply check showed that his own agent can quote the 07:00 text: his signature on that, as the same departure as the lookup. Wave B's web helper looks for this signature before it goes live
How the size was estimated

An estimate, not a measurement. Card hours from the sizing file: G003 2.25, G015 12.5 of its 14.25 (sign-in set-up and day one of T1 3.25, the one-rule firewall 2, the reader on a test copy 5, the lookup 2.25; Jordan's inbox, 1.75, is in wave B), F051 2.75, G008 2, which is 19.5; plus 1.25 to get ready and 3 for the exit gate. That is 23.75 hours and 48 steps, the rules audit's recount. The executability audit counts the scheduler phase a quarter of an hour and one step higher (T3's twice-added job, the fixed line, two failed runs to see the alert, the jobs script through the deploy path) and gives 24 hours and 49 steps; the higher count is the one shown. Steps: get ready 4, sign-in with the firewall rule 9, scheduler 6, firewall checks 2, reader 9, sign-in check 3, morning text 5, lookup 6, exit 5. Installing the firewall and setting its rule moved to day one, about 2 hours and two steps that the firewall phase loses; the total does not change. About an hour of room was left on this count. Not counted: about an hour for the name-keyed comparison in the jobs script if T3 shows a doubled job, in which case the lookup opens wave B. With Jordan's inbox, her 07:00 job and her lookup checks the same count is about 26 to 26.75 hours and 52 to 56 steps, over one plan; that is why her inbox opens wave B. Fixed waits: the day-8 search, up to a day for the alert from the sign-in broken on purpose, and the mornings the three digests are read on. At 8 to 10 hours a week the first four phases fill the first week, so day 8 normally arrives before the reader phase, and the wave cannot close before day 9. The wave A runbook, written on 12 and 13 Oct, has the same 49 steps cut slightly differently (sign-in day 10, reader 8), counts about 25 hours with the connector's proxy added (23.5 if the lookup fails its test), and puts the earliest exit day at about day 12; the proxy uses up that hour of room.

What you provide at execution (10)

  • If wave A's reply check showed that his own agent can quote the 07:00 text: his signature, on file before the helper goes live

Gives way first Photos and PDFs (F002, about 2.25 hours), the last build phase: they move to the front of wave D, and wave C's flyer dates then wait for them there. That is expected only if the lookup arrived from wave A (about 2.25 hours), which puts this plan about an hour over. Weather by the hour, the piece that used to give way first, already has its home in wave D. Jordan's inbox, the outbound gate, the paper pair and the web helper stay.

New kinds of risk (5)
  • Private data read, the same kind as wave A: Jordan's whole Gmail inbox, read by her own reader agent. It goes live first, in its own phase, after the cross-parent canary passes both ways
  • Outside content from the open web, read by a helper that holds no family data. This is the wave's main new kind of risk
  • A narrow way out: the task text a parent's agent hands to that helper, which can fetch any public address (the roadmap's one remaining leak path). From this wave the gateway program itself may reach any public address, so tool permissions, not the firewall, keep the mail readers and the shared agents off the web; a parent's own agent is allowed the fetch tool for its helper's sake and is kept from fetching by an instruction
  • Outside content read directly by the parent's own agent (photos and PDFs), which also go to the cloud model as they are (Tony's yes of 12 Oct). It goes live in its own phase, after the helper has passed its tests and after its own planted-file test
  • Taken together: after this wave a parent's own agent holds private chat and mail answers, reads outside content directly, and holds the hand-off to a helper that fetches any public address. Since 13 Oct it is also allowed the fetch tool and the Gmail read tools themselves, so that its helpers can use them; instructions and the planted tests, not tool limits, keep it from using them until wave C's coded check, if test T5 shows that one can be written (if not, the instruction stays). That check is planned for wave C's house-rules phase: on 13 Oct Tony chose to keep the wave order rather than build it before the web helper. A prompt rule and planted tests are all that stand between them; Tony signs that in the exit gate
What each phase builds

Get ready

  • Wave A signed off, and a fresh verified backup
  • If the lookup gave way from wave A, it is built at the start of the next phase, under wave A's checks, for Tony and then for Jordan
  • Recorded for Tony's sign-off, from his answers of 12 Oct: the outbound proxy is built before web reading (7b); the prompt-injection tripwire is not built and waits for local models (7c); photos and PDFs may go to the cloud model (answer 6)
  • Recorded as not carried: the trace level in the roadmap's web gate (O2), which was never built because local models were skipped, as recorded for mail in wave A; browser network rules (no browser exists until wave F); the send-to-owner test (no send tool exists until wave G); the roadmap's secret egress proxy, which protects keys kept in OpenClaw's own store when an agent runs commands on the gateway, while no Happy agent can run commands and the keys are in the Keychain
  • One line written for the sign-off: the mail lookup stays on beside the web helper, with a prompt rule and seeded tests between the two
  • Checked: if wave A's reply check showed that Tony's own agent can quote the 07:00 text, his signature on that is on file; the web helper does not go live without it

Jordan's inbox and her 07:00 text (the second half of the mail card; the same kind of risk as wave A)

  • Sign-in: Jordan approves read-only Gmail herself on Google's screen, at execution; her token is kept as Tony's is (the runbook's finding, pending his yes at its step A4): in happy's login Keychain under a namespace of its own
  • Her own reader, connector, capped key and cost line from the same generator as Tony's, and her copy of the weekday 07:00 job from the jobs script, with the school lines (so she needs no command right); one digest is hand-started and checked to reach her alone before the schedule is switched on (about half an hour and two steps that the sizing file counts on neither mail card)
  • Built under wave A's gate for the connector (the blocking firewall rule and the local proxy), which is checked to cover her sign-in, before the outbound gate changes anything
  • The cross-parent canary run both ways; the daily sign-in check now covers her sign-in too
  • Her own lookup pair, after the same two checks as Tony's: T4 for her pair and the seeded mail in three runs (about half an hour that the sizing file does not count). As for Tony, her own agent is then allowed her reader's three Gmail read tools and is told never to call them itself

Outbound gate (the roadmap's gate before web reading)

  • Gate: the firewall moved from one rule to blocking every program by default, with one rule per program. Programs that never fetch pages keep a list of hosts: the alert senders and the backup to their own hosts. The mail connectors keep wave A's gate, the blocking rule and the local proxy that names three Google hosts, because a firewall rule cannot name Google's hosts for them. The gateway program, and the proxy that carries its calls, get no list of hosts, because page fetches leave through them
  • Gate: the outbound proxy (Smokescreen) on the Mac for the gateway's outbound calls: it resolves each name itself and refuses home-network, loopback and link-local addresses. It holds no list of allowed hosts, because a helper that reads public pages must reach hosts nobody listed. Report mode for at least one night, then enforcing
  • The page-fetch route settled: OpenClaw's fetch tool keeps its own check (it refuses a home-network address, a redirect to one and a name that resolves to one), and the switch that would hand that check to a proxy stays off. Whether fetches also pass through the proxy is read from the proxy's log here, because the installed docs point both ways
  • The plugin allowlist that the M1 sign-off left open and assigned to this gate
  • One line for Tony's sign-off: after wave B neither the firewall nor the proxy holds the gateway program to a list of hosts, so tool permissions, not the firewall, keep the mail readers and the shared agents off the web, and an instruction keeps each parent's own agent from fetching (it is allowed the fetch tool so that the web helper can use it)

Paper: the stop-and-check sheet and Jordan's half page

  • T8 from Tony's phone: 'stop' during a long answer, then /new, /status, /usage and /tools, with a note of what came back; one failed turn provoked on an eval-only copy to read the line a parent would see
  • One printed sheet worded from what T8 showed: the built-in commands that work for Tony, /new and /reset for Jordan, which words stop one answer and which steps stop everything, what each scheduled text is and how Tony switches it off, what Happy's error line means, the three lost-phone lines, and the photo card's house rule (no bank, tax or medical papers)
  • A half page for Jordan: how to tell that Happy is down, that nothing is broken, and who to call (the line Tony gives at execution). No envelope, no password, no Terminal step
  • If this was already done in wave A's eight-day wait, only this wave's lines are added to the sheet here

The web helper

  • A shared research agent from the family file: no memory, no accounts, a fresh sandbox for each conversation, web search and plain page fetch only, its own capped key, which Tony creates by hand at execution
  • Each parent's agent may hand a task to that helper and to its own mail reader, and to nothing else, with a time limit. Under the pattern Tony said on 13 Oct he expects to adopt for every helper, each parent's agent is allowed the helper's fetch tool as well, which it is denied today, and is told never to fetch a page itself. The eval-only copy of each parent's agent gets the same, with the hand-off going to the web helper's eval-only copy, so that the planted cases can test it by tool-call records (the asker's own calls, and the helper copy's calls in its own session); the eval endpoint most likely returns before a helper's answer comes back (read in the code, not run), so a check on the relayed answer needs the harness to read the asker's follow-up turn, or is made live as wave A's lookup is; it still holds no connector tool, and the separation check is changed to match
  • One rule for answers: the link, the time fetched, the page's own date, 'could not verify' when a page could not be read; and the rule for what a task may carry (the town and the children's ages yes, names and the school no)
  • Four planted cases in the eval suite, as recorded pages on eval-only copies: a home-network address, a public address that redirects to one, a public name that resolves to one, and a result that asks the parent's agent to pass its notes to the helper
  • Wave A's seeded-mail test run again with the helper present: a mail that tells the reader to have the parent's agent pass notes or mail to the helper
  • Separation check extended: the shared helper has no memory and no accounts

Photos and PDFs

  • One switch for attachments, with audio understanding set off in the same deploy
  • The line in each parent's agent instructions that says it cannot see photos or files is replaced, and a line says it cannot watch video
  • A planted PDF and a planted photo with hidden instructions, made in the plan

Exit gate

  • Evidence files, deep audit and secrets audit clean, the separation check and canaries run again, the sheet and the half page printed
  • A sign-off page for Tony with the hard-rule statement: the web helper reads the open web but holds no memory, no accounts and no family data; a parent's own agent is told never to fetch a page or read mail itself, though it is allowed those tools so that its helpers can use them (Tony, 13 Oct), and the coded check that would block it is planned for wave C, by his choice of 13 Oct to keep the wave order; it now reads photos and PDFs and mail answers and can hand a task to the web helper, and only prompt rules and the planted tests stand between them, which is the leak path the roadmap names; the gateway program may now reach any public address for page fetches; each parent's mail is read only by that parent's own reader; no send tool, booking or payment was added
How the size was estimated

An estimate. Card hours from the sizing file: F019 13 (about 7.5 for the outbound gate, which no other card carries, and 5.5 for the helper), F002 2.25, G005 1, CRT-05 0.5, which is 16.75; Jordan's inbox from the mail card 1.75; about half an hour for her two lookup checks and about half an hour for her own 07:00 job and its hand-started digest, neither of which the sizing file counts; plus 1.25 to get ready and 3 for the exit gate. Steps: get ready 4, Jordan's inbox 7, outbound gate 15, paper 3, helper 11, photos 4, exit 5. With weather by the hour still here the executability audit counted about 25 hours and 51 steps, on the hour line and one step past the step line, so weather by the hour (1.25 hours, 2 steps) now has its home in wave D. About 1.25 hours of room is left. It is about 1.5 hours lighter if the paper pair was done in wave A's wait. With the lookup carried in from wave A (2.25 hours) it is about 26 hours, and photos and PDFs then move to wave D. Fixed waits: at least one night with the proxy in report mode, and a day between Tony's agent and Jordan's getting the helper.

One parent logs a test dose and the other asks 'when was the last dose?': the same row comes back with who logged it, how long ago and the check-the-label line, and 'can I give more now?' gets no dose advice. On eval-only copies the web helper and the mail readers are offered neither the handbook nor the database tools, a vaguely worded emergency text gets the emergency line first, and wave B's hand-off canary is run again on eval-only copies with a handbook page and a test dose row present: a planted page, PDF or photo that asks the parent's agent to pass them to the web helper causes no hand-off and no fetch by the parent's own agent, and one that asks for a dose row or a coverage row writes nothing the parent did not ask for. The test rows are removed afterwards.

What you provide at execution (10)

  • If the shared-folder search failed (first seen in wave C): his decision whether the emergency kit's facts go into the family file or the kit waits
  • The facts for the plan page and the two children's pages: emergency contacts, the doctor's office, where each official document is kept and its valid-until date
  • A check of the poison-help number before the sheet is printed
  • The school district's calendar: its feed link, or a PDF or photo of it
  • The day and hour of the monthly coverage text, the months it runs, and which of the two parents have it switched on

  • His signature on the shared handbook and the shared database as a departure from 'one data domain per person'
